2.	If so, what action has been taken by the Government as regards same?

A large number of petitions have been received, I think, by the House and some by the Government, protesting against the wet canteen being introduced at the camps in Canada, to which it would seem this question refers. Action was taken by the Government long ago in regard to the wet canteen in Canada, and there is nothing in this question to lead one to suppose that it refers to camps other than those in this country.

With your leave, Mr. Speaker, might I ask my hon. friend to supplement his answer. He says that action has been taken by the Government in regard to the camps in Canada. What action is being taken with regard to the camps overseas?
I did not take it that the question referred to camps overseas, but if my hon. friend would put his question in another form I should be glad to answer it.

* Mr. MURPHY:
1.	Has the attention of the Government been drawn to an alleged interview with Lieutenant-Colonel (Dr.) F. W. Marlow, published in the Toronto World on Wednesday, the 2nd instant, as follows :-
With reference to the articles emanating from Ottawa and appearing in the press on Saturday last, it may be said that there does not appear to have been any adequate reason why the parliamentary committee on returned soldiers should have been troubled with my letter of April 11, on the subject of an overseas appointment. It was directed to the officer in charge of administration at Toronto, and I presume a copy of it was forwarded to Ottawa, though not intended for public use.
Appointment Indefinite.
The reason for the letter was that in spite of reports from Ottawa that I was to go overseas to fill an important position in the Canadian Medical Service, I had been informed that no definite appointment could be given me before proceeding there, and that I might be given rank in the Canadian Expeditionary Force which, if accepted, would place me junior to a considerable number of medical officers who have entered the service since the war began, in spite of seventeen years of service in the Army Medical Corps and my two years of administrative work in the Toronto district.
It is unusual for medical officers proceeding overseas apart from organized medical units to be granted definite appointments before arrival there, but for nearly two years the vast majority of such as have gone over were newly appointed in the service and have gone over as reinforcements and with rank not higher than that of captain. On the other hand, in a few cases medical practitioners with little or no military experience have received definite appointments and high rank before going over. These also would rank senior to me, as two years' service on the staff at Toronto carried no standing in the Expeditionary Force towards the maintaining of which all the efforts of the staff were directed.
Considering such circumstances, and in view of my connection with the general problems of the medical service in Canada and also because of many recent events, particularly in connection with the problem of returned soldiers, I felt it my duty to defer accepting any overseas appointment until such time as the committee on returned soldiers reported to Parliament and likely discussions of the Medical Board were concluded, and especially as the appointment offered to me was of such indefinite and obscure character that its nature could not be revealed to me.
Statements to this effect were contained in my letter and an opportunity was sought for
discussing with the proper authorities the matter of an overseas appointment, but as yet such has not been granted.
Letter Made Public.
There was, so far as I can judge, nothing in the letter intimating that I had any expectation of being recalled by the Parliamentary Committee. For some reason, however, my letter was referred to them and consequently made public, with the result that the first and only reply to date came in the form of the newspaper article mentioned above, and also a letter from the chairman of the committee. Information through such channels was quite unexpected.
Having resumed my professional duties and as recent events are not likely to encourage me to accept any position at the hands of those responsible for my present relation to the service without a very careful investigation of the opportunities such position would afford for rendering useful service, I feel it my duty to "carry on" as at present and await further developments.
Meantime I shall watch with great interest the establishment of an effective plan for dealing with returned soldiers and will hope for the early inauguration of a united medical service and the emancipation of the same and the medical profession of Canada from the bondage placed upon them by laymen and politicians who deceive themselves in thinking they can get along without the doctors in dealing with medical problems or by relegating them, if called in, to a subordinate position which will not detract from the loftiness of their own altitude, in respect to matters requiring much technical knowledge, which they have never endeavoured to possess.
2.	Was Lieutenant-Colonel Marlow given an appointment in the Canadian Medical Service overseas?
3.	If so, what was the date thereof, and what were to be Dr. Marlowr's rank and duties?

2.	Yes. Lieut.-Col. Marlow was offered an appointment as llieutenant-colonel in the Army Medical Corps of the C. E. F. overseas, and provision wa3 made for him to sail.
3.	March 27, 1917. Dr. Marlow's rank was to be lieut.-colonel. His duties were to be allotted by the overseas military authorities on arrival, with due regard to his rank and qualifications and to the military exigencies.
4.	Hospital and medical units raised in Canada for the C. E. F. are provided with a specified establishment. Officers appointed to these units perform the duties of their appointment. Other officers not appointed to a specified unit, or to the staff, are detailed to the general li3t and allotted by the overseas authorities to duty in accordance

with their special qualifications and to the best advantage of the service.

That, in the opinion of this House, action should be taken by the Government at the earliest opportunity with a view to give effect to the recommendation of the Commission on Technical Education.

He said: Last session I brought forward a similar motion, my object being to obtain from the Government a statement of its policy with regard to this very important question. I failed in my effort then, at least partly. But, as the war draws to an end-I hope-it is of the utmost urgency that the Government should now make a decision as regards the report which was placed in their hands by the commission appointed a few years ago to investigate this subje'ct of technical education. I shall not dwell at length to-day upon this subject, because it has been pretty well exhausted in the many debates in this House in former sessions. Every one is seized of the need of a forward movement in this *matter. The urgency of thie question, its paramount importance, has been recognized by older countries. And, if it is urgent for older countries, it is still more urgent for a young country like Canada. Although very important strides have been made 'by Great Britain, France, Holland, and even by Japan, of late years, yet we must admit that it is to Germany we look as a model in this movement. A few months ago Lord Haldane spoke in England on this subject-and we know that Lord Haldane knows more about Germany than any of us in this House. He spent many years in German universities, and is a well-known authority on German education system generally. He said: I
I want to sound a warning of what is in store for us, I am more afraid of an engine for conquest in peace time which the Germans were busy preparing before the war, than I am of the 42-centimetre guns. This engine is educational. The most modern form of continuation school is extending itself over a large part of Germany, and it is planned to extend it over the whole Empire. It is a work school for imparting trade skill and general knowledge, rather than a mere book school, and it behooves us to be prepared for the shock of this competition which is coming after the war.
Germany is training the youth of the land in special skilled trades, to outdistance competitors throughout the world.
Mr. Speaker, I<say again, we must admit that Germany has led the world as regards technical education during the last half century. However, in England, and especially in Scotland, scientists and educationists have called the attention of the public to the necessity of a more perfected system of technical education. May I be permitted to quote the opinion of a famous scientist, engineer, builder and educator? I refer to J. Scott Russell who, as far back as 1869, used the following words which may apply to the conditions of to-day just as much as they 
applied to the conditions of England and Great Britain generally fifty or sixty years ago:
In every country-
Said Mr. Russell,
-where technical education has taken root and had time to bear fruit I also find unquestionable proofs of the rapidity with which increased intelligence and enlarged knowledge bring- increase in employment and remuneration. From my personal experience I may say that within the last twenty-five years I have seen large branches of commercial trade leave our country and plant themselves in another because the workers of the one were educated and those of the other uneducated. And I have watched nations rising into importance-
No doubt he was referring to Germany.
-and power by education and by order, organization, and efficiency, which education bestows, and other nations lagging behind and losing their place by reason of their unwillingness to educate either the higher or lower classes of their people.
Knowledge and mental discipline alone do not constitute education. To be practical and useful to all those who must earn their livelihood, education must also afford physical dexterity with special reference to the industrial pursuits of life. That is, in a word, the object of manual training and, in the highest sense, of technical education. It contributes to the development of the country, to its increased wealth and to the perfection of its citizens. There is also, in regard to this question of technical education a moral aspect which must not be lost sight of and, in this respect, I am pleased to see before me my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) because I am sure that the statistics which are at his disposal in the department over which he presides, will enable him to corroborate what I will state here. If one will consult the labour exchanges and the labour bureaus he will learn that the unemployed are generally the unskilled labourers. In that connection let me recall that phrase of Carlyle's, " that for a man to die ignorant who has the capacity for knowledge is a tragedy." In modern society all facilities should be given to the poor man to get his manual training. I have said that generally amongst the unemployed are to be found the unskilled labourers. I think I am right in stating that criminals are generally to be found amongst the unemployed and therefore the diminution of crime would be one of the beneficial results of a better technical education. According to the criminal statistics, I am told, one-third of all criminals are totally unedu-

*rated and four-fifths are practically uneducated. From that point of view alone, it seems to me that it is the duty of the Government to see that manual training and technical education are spread as much as possible amongst the labourers so as to avoid such a condition of things as is revealed in the criminal statistics of this and other countries. From the national point of view, the protection of our political institutions demands that the industrial education of our youth be intensified so that they may carry with them our ideas of obedience to law and the principles of democratic government in the midst of the multitude of foreigners who crowd our factories and mines and perform much of our labour.
Coming back to the effect of technical education on the various industries of the country, let me say broadly that the manufacturer is aided by industrial education in the improvement of his product. His success depends on the demand for his goods at reasonable prices. His activities are regulated by the needs of his customers. They ask generally for durability of material, attractiveness of design, excellence of workmanship, and all these, Mr. Speaker, I contend, can be secured and secured only by the application of technical knowledge and manual training.
Let me say, en passant, that on various occasions the Manufacturers Association of Canada, a very powerful body, has passed resolutions asking the Governments, both Federal and Provincial, but especially the Federal Government, to implement what has been done in the various provinces in the way of improving the system of technical education.
Having spoken of the effect of technical knowledge upon manufacturing, let me say now what, in my judgment, would be the effect on the working classes. Aside from the moral and religious education which, of course, must be paramount, the technical education of the working classes has the inevitable result of elevating their condition. Industrial education dignifies labour. If labour has a noble end and purpose, if it employs intellect, if it abundantly rewards its servants, then it is worthy to toe crowned. The perfection of our manufacturing, the facilitating of commerce, the unearthing of mineral wealth, the thorough exploitation of farms, the dissemination of practical knowldege, are the ends which are toeing served by technical education. Whilst the various provinces have of late years been responsive to the demands made
by the Manufacturers Association and by labour generally, a great deal remains to be done. I must pay homage to the great province of Ontario for the remarkable progress it has made in technical education. I am told by my friends who represent that province, that the Technical Institute of Toronto is second to none; and I know, as a matter of fact, that many years ago Nova Scotia, that little province by the sea -little in size but great by the men it has sent to Parliament and has given to Canada-has also toeen a pioneer in technical education. When my late colleague, the Hon. Mr. Fielding, was Prime Minister of Nova Scotia, he, by the subsidizing of a Technical Institute, gave to the progress of that province, which is so rich in mineral deposits and in coal mines especially, an impetus which will never be forgotten; and he thereby incidentally gave to the country a corps of mining engineers second to none in America.
Having spoken of Ontario and Nova Scotia and knowing something of what is being done in the Western Provinces, I can say with pride that in the province of Quebec to-day, substantial progress is being made in that direction. It is not a party question with us; the two parties, and I am pleased to say the two races and all creeds in the province of Quebec, have united in support of a splendid system of technical education. We have the Montreal Technical School, the Quebec Technical School, the Beauceville Technical School, and the Shawinigan Falls Technical School and others. We have in those schools many hundreds of students, and it is remarkable that since the beginning of the war, where in the various shell manufacturing establishments experts and instructors have been required, the men who came out of the Montreal Technical School have taken the first places. Giving my own personal experience, let me say that a year ago I met, in the county of Drummond, a young man, the son of a well-to-do farmer of St. Germain de Grantham. He was introduced to me after a religious service on Sunday by the father, who said: "My lad has just received his diploma from the Technical School in Montreal, and I wonder what I will do with him now." I said: "You have many opportunities open for him at the present time because in every shell manufactory you can find employment for your boy." He went to Montreal and got his son into the shell manufactory of Lymburner and Co. Five or six months

afterwards I received a visit from the young man, and I asked him if he was satisfied with his position and he answered that he was. I asked him how much he earned a day, and he said he earned $8 per day. Because of his technical knowledge he had become instructor to the army of shell makers in that large munition plant. This is only to illustrate what immense good technical institutes in our provinces and elsewhere can accomplish.
I am quite aware that there is a standing objection against this Parliament dealing with the question of technical education. I know that under section 93 of the British North America Act education comes under exclusive provincial jurisdiction, and you are well aware, Mir. Speaker, that I generally stand for provincial rights; that I would not have this Parliament encroach on any of the subject matters which are within provincial jurisdiction. But we have a military college which, apart from purely military matters, is heavily subsidized by this Parliament. We grant subsidies, at least we did a few years ago, to exclusively provincial railway companies. We have a naval school at Halifax in your own province, Mr. Speaker. The Department of the Interior receives from this Parliament a subsidy to spread the knowledge of the metric system in Canada. This Parliament has granted to the various provinces, towards the improvement of Agriculture, the sum of, I think, $10,000,000; so that on the whole the Dominion Government could find a way, if there is a will, to co-operate with the provinces and make grants towards industrial training and technical education.
I do not know that I should not address myself more especially this afternoon to the right hon. Minister pf Trade and Commerce rather than to the Minister of Labour. Perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce would he more responsive than my hon. friend the Minister of Labour was last year. However, I shall address myself to the 'Government generally and to the House.
Sir, this matter affects primarily trade and commerce. It affects our manufactured products as to their quality, quantity, and the means of transportation, and, on the whole it is a question of national concern. The Dominion Government could, therefore, without encroaching on provincial Tights, co-operate with the provincial authorities and thereby help to give a better technical training to our yeomanry. I may he told
[Mr. I.emieux.l
that the provinces have their own revenues which they may well apply to the cause of technical education. Well, the revenues of the provinces are derived virtually-I was going to say chiefly-from Dominion subsidies, nearly $12,000,000 being transferred each year from the Dominion exchequer to the provinces. I am pleased to say that the good old province of Quebec has apart from its share of subsidies, an excellent financial standing. As hon. gentlemen can see for themselves if they look at the figures in connection with the loans recently made by the Allied -Governments on the New York market, the province of Quebec is financially in splendid shape. I noticed the other day with great pleasure and great pride that one of the loans launched by Great Britain and another one by France on the New York market were to have as collateral 'securities the bonds of the province of Quebec, which rank as high as the bonds of the Dominion Government, if not higher. Sir, the revenues of the provinces, being derived chiefly from subsidies, are, however, somewhat strained by provincial needs, and you cannot develop a system of technical education such as we require in order to deal effectively with the problems that will arise immediately after the conclusion of the war if the matter its left entirely to the provinces. From their comparatively slender sources of revenue, the provinces have to maintain public services of great importance, such as the administration of justice, the maintenance of civil rights, the care of the public domain, roads and bridges, the organization and supervision of municipal government, and the organization, administration and -support of general -education.
I have said that the provinces could not very well, from their slender revenues, organize as they should the system of tech nical education which we dream of for this country. Dr. James W. Robertson, of Ottawa, a good Scotchman-I have -a weakness for Scotchmen-in an address delivered in the month of April, 1915, made the following statement with regard to the probable expenditure that the organization of a system of technical education in Canada on a safe basis would entail:
In making a forecast of the probable cost of maintaining an adequate system of industrial training and technical education, the Commission considered the populations and need of 566 places in Canada, besides the rural population in the counties. These 566 places, ranging from great cities like Montreal and Toronto down to incorporated villages of over 500 people, contained a total population of

2,790,000. In these urban places the number of persons between 14 and 17 years of age who were not attending any day school is estimated at 150,000 young people. The population of Canada according to the last census, outside of the 566 places already indicated, amounted to 4,400,000, of whom 237,000 are young persons between the ages of 14 and 17 not attending any school. If the proportion of attendance of these 387,000 young people could be brought up to that of many areas in England, Scotland and Ireland, no less than 213,000 of them would be continuing their education at suitable classes after they had begun to earn their living.
From that statement made by Professor Robertson, it looks as if the cost of technical education, spread throughout all those localities in Canada, would be rather high if undertaken by the provinces, I quite grant that by section 93 of the British North America Act, education is assigned exclusively to the provinces and that there is actually no dividing line between technical education and what is generally called cultural education. But surely we can do something towards stimulating the interest of our people in this subject. If I mistake not, this is the broad conclusion reached by the commissioners who were appointed a few years ago to investigate this question.
Do not forget, Mr. Speaker-the figures given the other day by the Minister of Finance prove this-that Canada is, after all, during these years of wiar enjoying a fictitious prosperity. The time will soon .come, I hope, when we shall revert to our ordinary vocations. The problem of the aftermath, it seems to me, is one which should arouse the attention of this Parliament and I do not see how we can better help our .people to grasp that problem than by doing something practical for technical education and manual training in Canada.
Thousands of soldiers will soon return to Canada. Some of them, I hope, will settle on the land; but much as I would like to see our soldiers become sturdy farmers of the West and of the East, I have not much faith in soldiers as farmers, and I am here expressing a current opinion based on past experience. There were given in this House the other evening figures in regard to the returned soldiers after the South African war, and we know what was done with the land scripts which they received. At all events, thousands of soldiers will come back to Canada; they will find that the war industries have disappeared, let us hope, for ever and ever; they will also find the old industries of the country dislocated, and it will take all the grit and all the energy
and all the statesmanship of our Governments to restore pre-war industrial conditions. It seems to me that the time is now ripe for Canada to look to the future and to do something to equip our returned soldiers for the battle of life.
Last year I quoted extensively from the report of a commission appointed by the Ontario Government and presided over by Sir John Willison, and one of the chief conclusions of that report was that Canada had to do two Jhings in order to maintain its name, its traditions, and its credit after the war: first, to capture as much trade as possible, and second, to equip for the battle of bread winning our returned soldiers and our young men by giving them a first class technical knowledge. In^Great Britain the Government is quite alive to this very important issue. The question came up in the British House of Commons in 1916 on a motion by Mr. Hewins. I have already quoted what was said in that discussion by such authorities as Sir Alfred Mond and Mr. Walter Runciman, who was then President of the Board of Trade, and I wish now to quote a few sentences from the speech of Mr. Lynch. He said:
In the course of time with the development of civilization, other - nations have entered into the lists as competitors, and before this war, England was being hard pressed by Germany. The foundation of the prosperity which Germany enjoyed before the war was laid generations ago. I will take the turning point, that of the advent of Wilhelm Von Humboldt to the position of Director of Public Instruction, in the year 1809. He was not a politician in the ordinary sense, but a man of very wide learning and imbued with the scientific spirit. He was called by the Prussian nation to establish a system of education, and in two years he laid the foundation of a system of education which has been the real root and source of the prosperity which Germany subsequently enjoyed. I will here point out that those in this country who occupy a position corresponding to that held by Wilhelm Von Humboldt have never been chosen as great educationists. At the present moment it would be hard for any honourable member of this House to say who is our Minister of Education, for he is suspended, like Mohamet's coffin, between Heaven and, say, the earth. The man who held this position in Germany for two years exercised such a wide influence and power that the reverberations of his efforts are felt for a century afterwards, while some of our educationists, if they had been in power a hundred years, would not have left their reverberations for a succeeding two years. For that I blame the Government.
I have read very carefully the debate on the co-operation of the Allies in the war, and the minds of the British House of Commons declared that in order
4 p.m. to capture the trade which before the war belonged to Germany,

England would have to repeat the history of Germany in the matter of technical education.
We have discussed this question on many occasions. In 1909, one of the -ablest speeches I ever -heard was delivered on that very question -by my hon. friend the -member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), ' whom I am pleased to see hack in his -seat after having been absent because of illness. T-h-e hon. -member on that occasion delivered a most elaborate address, which had quite an effect on the House and- on the country. Several hon. members took -part in the debate, amongst others the right hon. the Prime Minister.
The resolution introduced by my hon. friend for South Wellington read:
That in the opinion of this House it is advisable that a commission of inquiry be forthwith appointed to investigate the needs of Canada in respect of technical education, and to report on ways and means by which these needs may be best met.
The Minister of Labour -at that time was the Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, whose knowledge on questions of this kind is admitted by all. He also delivered a very important speech, and as a result of that debate, in the session of 1910 an appropriation was made on May 3 for the expenses of the inquiry. An Order in Council was passed, and the commissioners were appointed. Correspondence also took -place between the Minister of Labour and the provincial governments, whi-oh will be found in the report. The work of the -commission was very exhaustive, and is contained in a voluminous report of four volumes which deals with the question in a most exhaustive way. The commission was presided over by Professor Robertson, who is a well known authority not only in Canada but throughout the world. The commission visited 100 places in Canada, held 175 -sessions, heard evidence from 1,470 witnesses, men and women, -some of whom occupied foremost positions in industry, agriculture, house-keeping, and technical education generally. The commissioners also went beyond Canada and pursued their investigations in England, Scotland, Ireland, Denmark, France, Germany, Switzerland and the United States. They were given the amplest opportunity for investigation; everywhere, as they say in their report, they met with courtesy and enthusiasm. They found an increased interest in technical education. The countries which had taken the deepest interest in the matter were striving to do better still; in a w'ord, the most advanced were the least

satisfied. It is useless for me to go into the details of that report, which is in the possession of every hon. member, but it may be well that I should remind
the House that the published conclusions of ^ the commission have not yet been acted upon, and my object in rising was to ask the Government and my hon. friend the Minister of Labour what they intend to do in regard to those conclusions. When the question was under discussion in 1909 the opinion of the present Prime Minister, then leader of the Opposition, was expressed in no uncertain language. Brushing aside the objection that had been raised by some hon. members, that the Parliament of Canada could not investigate matters of education, or -appropriate funds for that purpose, because, forsooth, it was a question within the jurisdiction of the provinces, he said:-
If the position of the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) be correct the Government has been violating the constitution of Canada for 35 or 40 years in the establishment of the Military Scnool in Kingston. But I have not heard of any province raising any objection. But the hon. minister need not stop at the Kingston military school, let him look at the estimates of this year or any year, and he will find over and over again, where the Government has spent money by the million on matters absolutely within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. Does not my hon. friend know that his own estimates which he has just brought down, contain dozens of items for aid to undertakings purely local and absolutely within the- jurisdiction of the local legislatures? Local works and undertakings, except in so far as they connect one province with another or some province with a country outside Canada, are purely and absolutely within provincial control, yet you can take the estimates and on page after page you will find money given by the $5,000, $10,000 and $100,000 to undertakings of that kind. The Parliament of Canada has the right to vote money for any purpose that it may deem proper. It has voted money for purposes absolutely outside Canada. For example, to aid the sufferers at San Francisco, to industrial exhibitions without our own country, subsides to provincial railways which are purely works of a local character, and under provincial jurisdiction, aid to art schools, special lectures upon the advantages of the metric system, a grant to McGill university in aid of work of this kind, schools for the examinations of masters and mates, to keep up the school at Kingston and for the establishment of experimental farms.
He concluded -as follows:-
I have thought it desirable to place this aspect of the question before the House. I say to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that I am entirely in sympathy with the object he has in view, and I trust action will be taken along the line he has suggested, if no other action can he taken, hut so far as I am concerned I would greatly and infinitely prefer that a more definite and practical and speedy action should be taken than that which has been suggested in this resolution itself.

So the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Trade and Commerce need have no scruples, because the Prime Minister, in the speech I have just quoted, practically gave him his fiat in 1909. To recapitulate. The resolution was introduced by my hon. friend for South' Wellington, and the appropriation for the commission was voted at the following session in 1910. The commissioners were appointed, and visited nine countries. They heard 1,400 witnesses in Canada, and held hundreds of sessions both in this country and outside. They published a very voluminous report in four volumes, and in their conclusions asked this Government to co-operate with the provinces in this matter. Yet the report has been shelved. Nothing has been done. We are all looking forward to the cessation of hostilities ; we expect this war to end soon, and our soldiers will then be returning by the hundreds of thousands; we know that it is our duty to equip these soldiers for the battle of life; we talk about capturing the trade of other countries, especially that of enemy nations. And yet, although all these facts are well known, the Government has done nothing. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour says that the report is in his department, and that he is awaiting instructions from the various provincial governments.
It seems to me this a most urgent question, and that the Government should, once for all, take action on this report which has cost so much money and labour-though not too much, in my opinion. The Government should declare that the spread of technical skill and knowledge will .be subsidized by the Dominion in co-operation with the various provinces. At page 21 of the report of the commission appears the following:
The Underlying Principles.
The Commission is of the opinion that Industrial Training and Technical Education in order to he of greatest benefit to individuals, to industrial development, to localities, to the several provinces, and to the Dominion as a *whole, should be organized and maintained in accordance with the following principles:-
1.	It should be under provincial control and regulation.
2.	It should receive financial support from individuals, from local authorities, from provincial governments, and from the Dominion.
3.	Provision should be made for active participation in its control, management and direction by individuals in the locality who would represent industries as employers and employees, agriculture, women's occupations, particularly housekeeping, business, and organized education.
4.	It should provide educational opportunities for those who have gone to work and also for those who are able to return and devote their
time for some months or years, as the case may be, to a course or courses of instruction and training.
5.	It should make provision to ensure, as far as practicable, equality of opportunity for all preparing for industrial, agricultural and housekeeping occupations, and for workers in such occupations.
6.	It should be carried on in cordial cooperation with existing systems of education, and in such a way as to have the advantage of the use of existing buildings, equipment and teaching staff so far as these may be suitable and available.
Once more, in bringing this motion to the attention of the House, I sincerely hope that the Government will not fail to decide upon such a policy in this matter as will improve the opportunities open to our own people and will also help to settle some of the gravest problems which will arise after the war.
Last winter an address was delivered by Dr. H. E. Howe, to which was given the very apt title "The German Alarm Clock." In opening, the speaker said:
However alert we may he individually, it has required the efforts of the biggest alarm clock in history to arouse us collectively to the dangers which beset us, and to the methods by which we were being placed in a subordinate position.
As I said a moment ago, that which gave Germany its trade and industrial preponderance in the world was the technical knowledge which, for almost a century, has been given to young Germans. Dr. Howe proceeds:
Prior to the war, Germany was carefully, - patiently and persistently conducting a successful commercial conquest of the world. Her agents were everywhere occupying positions of low as well as high degree according to the requirements of their particular task, learning the language of the country in which they worked, making themselves familiar with market and trade conditions, and reporting constantly to the great organizations at home, in order that no detail might be overlooked in giving them a firm hold upon world markets. I am informed that German concerns were even supplying the great bulk of chains, anchors and similar equipment to the maritime country of Great Britain. Through the co-operation which existed between the government, manufacturers, and banks, German salesmen were often able to make terms of credit quite impossible with a manufacturer not having such beneficent aid.
In another paragraph he said:
I hope this gives some idea of the condition of affairs when the war first broke out in August, 1914. As soon as the German fleet disappeared from the seas the various countries suddenly awakened as if by an alarm clock to the extent of their dependence upon German products. For the first time many people began to analyse the situation to learn the cause of Germany's strong position in many lines, and

I think all have come to the conclusion that the three principal causes at least are education, organization and scientific research.
I shall not quote any more. I think I have said enough to become myself tihe " alarm clock " of the Minister of {Labour. I want him to give the House and the country the promise that he will take down from the shelf the report of this commission and apply himself during the coming holiday to finding a solution of this question by inviting-should there be any objection from that quarter-the premiers or the Ministers of Education of the several provinces, to confer with him, and, while co-operating with them, lead in this cause of technical education in Canada.
I hope I have not kept the House too long. But I sincerely believe that this is a most acute problem, that of giving to our young men, our returned soldiers, the arms and the weapons with which during the era of peace which will succeed the era of war, Canada, through them and by them, shall take its true place amongst the progressive nations of the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in almost identical
words, my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has reminded us of the speech delivered in this House just a year ago, which will be found at page 2177 of last year's Hansard. My reply will be found at page 2187 of last year's Hansard. I do not propose to follow his example and take up an hour repeating what I said a year ago. I think our attitude was made fairly clear at that time and it has not materially changed sinee as far as I am aware. I do not know where my hon. friend got the idea that I was not very enthusiastically in favour of technical and industrial education. 1 do not yield to him for one moment in that respect. I realise the great advantages that would accrue from a more thorough system of technical education and industrial training than we have at the present time. I think that if my hon. friend's memory had been a little more reliable he would have had in his mind something of what I said last year. It will be found at page 2187. I am only going to read a sentence or two:	.
So that it seems to me that the question before us is not whether technical education and industrial training are desirable-indeed, are of the highest national importance, and should be brought within the reach of every youth in the land-but rather how best can these advantages be placed before them. The Government is quite alive to the importance

of practical as well as cultural education, and realizes that inestimable advantages would accrue to Canada had every youth an opportunity of acquiring technical education and training in the particular vocation chosen for his or her life work. Especially, I think, do we owe it to the mechanic, the artisan, and other wage earners, to provide them an opportunity to qualify themselves for larger earning power and to take a more prominent and influential place in the various activities in which our people are engaged.
That was my view on the question at t'hat time and I have not changed it since. As my hon. friend has said, there are difficulties surrounding this question. He has told us that education, under our constitution, is exclusively assigned to the various provinces. He knows from what I said last year that when the report of the Commission on Technical Education and Industrial Training, to which he has referred, was printed and bound, it was forwarded to each of the provincial governments with a request for an expression of opinion concerning the suggestions made in that report. I think I am safe in saying that in the replies that we got there was only one provincial government in Canada that approved of the system set forth in the report. That "was, if I remember aright, the province of Nova Scotia, as represented by the premier of that province. Now, I am not going into the particulars as to these objections because there they are set forth in Hansard and I do not think I would be warranted in taking up the time of the House for an hour in repeating what I said last year. An Association exists in Canada that has for its special object the encouragement of technical education and industrial training. It held a meeting in Toronto a year ago last October and this was part of a resolution passed by that association specially interested in the development of this question:
It is necessary and expedient that financial assistance be rendered by the Dominion to the several provinces for the service of technical education, as soon as the Government is freed from the pressing problems of the present war.
The men specially interested in this question thought that no such application should be made to this Government until they had become freed from the responsibilities and expenditures of the present war. We are not free yet; the expenditures are larger than they were a year ago. A great deal has been, and is being, done by the various provinces, as my hon. friend has already stated, more perhaps by the three provinces of Ontario, Quebec, and Nova Scotia, than the others. I think that

last year my hom. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) said that we were committed to the idea of rendering financial assistance in some way ot other but not at that time. That is my position to-day. I sympathize as deeply as the hon. member for Rouville can sympathize with the idea of encouraging technical education and I realise the great advantage it would be to all classes in this country if we had a more extensive, a more thorough, system of technical education and industrial training, but I do not think this is the time to take it up. I do not think we would be warranted in doing so and I can only say now that I sympathize with the idea of extending and making more thorough the system of technical education and that we will be prepared to render assistance of some sort, in some way, when the proper time comes, but in our judgment we would not be warranted in making such a large expenditure as is recommended in this report while the war is on.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) has repeated to this House what he said last year. Of course, he does not go over all the letters that he had last year from the different provinces, stating approval or objection to the proposals. I admit that he iis right in not doing so. I notice on the Order Paper to-day that there is a Bill to be introduced for good roads. I do not know how much it is proposed to devote to this object but I suppose it will be $10,000,000. We are at war at the present time and will be at war for a long time to come. From a financial standpoint, we are going to be at war for a great many years. If we wait until the finances of the country are in an absolutely settled condition before we grant a sum of money to each province for technical education, none of us will see it, because we will not live that long. There is a generation at present growing up who are absolutely in need of technical education. Nothing is so important to-day as technical education. We have to look to the future, and it is clear that we must have greater production from our men. We hear every day in the House of the number of producers who are giving their lives in the war, millions of men. If that is so, then we are justified in saying that we will need more production from the young boys who are now ready to receive technical education. In the past we have had to go across the water to get professors and men of 79
technical knowledge. It is unnecessary to enter into details as to the need for technical education, because that is admitted by both sides. The present Prime Minister (Sir Robert Boiden), when he was leader of the Opposition, acknowledged as one of the greatest lawyers in the country, said that this Parliament would be within its rights in granting aid to technical education. We are just as entitled to do that to-day when my right hon. friend is at the head of the Government. Furthermore, I do not know that there is anything in the constitution of the country which would prevent any Federal Government making grants to the provinces for such a purpose.
Without going into details of what happened in the House last year when the Good Roads Bill was under consideration, it was proven then that it would have been adopted by the House had the money been granted to the different provinces according to population. What is to prevent the Government following that plan in respect to technical education? The Minister of Labour says that according to some resolution which has been passed we should concern ourselves about technical education until we have settled our financial problems. But surely if there was a grant to each province according to its population, the association which has passed this resolution would surely be only to glad to see that it was put into operation.
The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Le-mieux) has spoken of different technical schools. I happen to know something about one because I am a member of the commission having charge of the Montreal school. The difficulty which that commission has in securing the funds necessary for the administration of the schopl going to the city and going to the provincial government to secure money, is far beyond the imagination of many of the members of this House. We have to gather money for the war from many different sources, we are doing that to-day, and we still have to gather money for technical education. As I have said before the recommendation of the Royal *Commission was that $3,000,000 should be voted for the promotion of technical education. The Minister of Labour will never make me or any other man of common sense believe that if a sum less than this was granted a province would not accept it. Let the 'Government show their willingness to do something to assist teolmical education. If we are going to wait until



this Government or any other Government is in a position to settle all the financial affairs of the country, to put them ,on a solid footing, before dealing with technical education, we are going to make the greatest mistake of our lives in reference to the future of the country.

Mr. 'Speaker, the hon. gentleman
who has just spoken summed up the whole matter in his reference to the fact that both sides of the House were of opinion that technical education was a matter of first importance, and something that must be dealt with as soon as possible. He overlooks one matter, however, to which I expected the Minister of Labour to refer, that the Prime Minister of this country (Sir Robert Borden) was the means of having appointed, since last session, a body of experts for the purpose of looking into this matter from a purely Canadian point of view. The report which we had laid upon the table of the House last year was very voluminous, very thorough, and enabled all those who took an interest in the subject to thoroughly inform themselves. This being the case, after a required period for digestion, it was agreed upon by everybody that if Canada desired to continue doing well and intended to do better, she must take further steps. But in scientific matters it is not possible to proceed by sudden fits and starts; it is necessary to consider these things thoroughly and carefully, and they can only be properly and adequately considered by those who are thoroughly qualified to consider them. That being the idea actuating the Prime Minister, and quite properly so as I am sure we all agree, he appointed a board presided over, I think, by Professor Mackenzie of Toronto University, to look into this very matter and to suggest what ought to be done, not only to look into it theoretically but also to give practical suggestions. There can be no question that an educated people is not only a better people mechanically considered, but intellectually and morally as well. If education is the basis of our advance and of the progress of civilization, why then it goes without saying that we should furnish for our people, especially for the great mass of our people, that intelligent and comprehensive understanding of their duties which alone makes success assured and life itself really worth living.
I do not like to hear such frequent references to the captures we are going to

make; this capturing of trade and capturing of other people all the time is repellent to me. Let us do our duty in the premises. Let us make ourselves better men and our country a better country, and we will have succeeded to the best of our ability and in a way that will leave us open to no criticism.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that I did not hear my hon. friend from Rouville this afternoon. I should have liked to have heard the course he has suggested that Parliament should take in this matter. I do not wish to say anything in reference to technical education to embarrass the Government at this particular time, because the one burning question with which we have to deal is this terrible war. But since this question has come up this afternoon, I wish to say that it is one that has puzzled me many and many a time. I have felt the need of technical education very severely in connection with the business in which I am now engaged. Just when and where to apply it puzzles me a little. May I put my difficulty this way: has our present system of education been the means of depleting the farms of agricultural help, and the factories of its mechanics? I would say candidly that it has. I shall never forget a statement made to me by a judge shortly after he had been appointed to the bench. He said that one of the most difficult things he had to contend with was the necessity of dealing with lawyers brought before him for debt. Would that not lead you to believe that our present educational system is depleting our supply of all kinds of mechanics and is over-crowding the professions? I want to give you the experience of the county in which I live. I cannot say that more than 5 per cent of the young men who went through our high school ever went .back to the farms or factories. Why was this the case? It is a problem that I cannot solve. I never could understand why a high school education should not better fit a man for work on the farm, and I know very well that a high school education would better fit him to go back to the factory. But they do not go back, and that is one of the reasons why I am puzzled to know just where technical education should be applied. Whether it could be imparted in our public schools or high schools. I do not know. At any rate, it has to be applied somewhere, because at present our educational system, although

it is said to be one of the finest in the world, is not supplying the farm and the factory with the help that they so much need.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
speechtext:
I have listened with interest to
the speech delivered by the horn, gentleman who has just taken bis seat (Mr. Thoburn). It is rather difficult to follow my hon. friend's reasoning. Followed in one direction, his argument suggests that we should have no education at all; that the man who is in absolutely raw condition is the best for the country's greater needs; that if a man has no education he will stay on the farm and work in the factory. Therefore, he should be given no education, in order that he may be kept in the factory or on the farm. I am sure that that is not what the hon. gentleman means; but that would be the substance of one line of his reasoning, because he suggests that if young people are given an education, they forsake occupations and activities which must necessarily be kept up.
As to my hon. friend's difficulty with regard to when this education should be given, all I can say is that I come from a country where we do give that education, not in its highest form, of course, but in a sort of primitive way. We have, it is true, a technical college in the province of Nova Scotia, where, during the past seven or eight years, the highest forms of technical education have been given, but the technical education that is of vast importance to the steel maker, coal miner and mining engineer is given in night schools. Professors of our colleges and academies are at the head of these night schools and are furnished with the necessary appliances and machinery by the use of which they give instruction in the making of engines, the production and application of electricity and the generating of power. In these schools we have trained an army of technical miners, technical steel makers, men who can handle and apply power, such as electricity; men who understand the proper production of power from coal. All the necessary work that is done in a coal mine and in connection with the production of iron and steel is taught in these schools. I assume that the same sort of thing is being done in the province from which my hon. friend comes. We should like to be carrying on this work on a larger scale, though we have, of course, taken an advanced step by establishing a technical college. This college is working in co-operation with other educational institutions. When a young 79}
man has taken two years in Dalhousie, for instance, he gets credit for them in the technical college, and after an additional two years in the technical college he may be graduated as a mechanical, electrical or civil engineer, according to the line that he may have followed. From this plan we have obtained very practical and very useful results. I think one of the reasons why young men leave the farm, or refuse to stay in the factory, is that they are kept at unproductive and what they consider to be uninteresting work. If they were able to secure a scientific knowledge of farming, of fisheries, of work in the factory, they would find these activities more congenial and more interesting than they find them now.
I submit to the Government, and particularly to the Minister of Labour, that it is not a sufficient answer to the suggestions of the member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) to say that 'last year and the year before the matter was before the House and the minister refused to do anything. It is not sufficient for the minister to look back to the years in which nothing was done and say: that is my record, and I am standing by it. That should not be a satisfactory answer if the Government as a whole are anxious for progress. Technical education is as much a war measure as anything else that is done in connection with the war. We cannot have too much technical knowledge of the elements entering into the various products and manufactures by the use of which we are assisting in carrying on the war. The making of shells, the proper production of power and of everything that enters into the manufacture of shells, guns and other war necessaries, can best be carried on by men who have technical education. This being the case, even under the War Measures Act, moneys could weill be applied for the encouragement of technical education in Canada.
We are wasting millions of dollars worth of property in this country from year to year because of the lack of technical education and fine tastes as to what uses can be made of our raw materials. If there is in this House a lumberman or a man who has knowledge of lumbering in some parts of this province, he will know the horrible and awful waste that occurs in our forests by reason of the fact that proper technical knowledge is not brought to bear upon lumber. Any one who knows anything about the fisheries of this country and the crude way in which we handle fish knows that although we secure millions of tons of fish and own millions of dollars worth of

property connected with the fishing industry, we throw away a great deal, probably a third, of the values that can be produced from our fisheries because we really do not know how to handle fish and do not know how to deal with the byproducts. Technical education along the line of teaching the people what are the byproducts of fish, how to handle fish and how best to put it on the market, would make our fisheries ten times as valuable as they are to-day. I have been told that in Newfoundland, where for years they had copper mines, they are reviving them again, because it has been found that millions of dollars worth of copper were thrown away simply because the people there had not the proper appliances to deal with the copper products. Our coal mines and our steel works are in much the same condition; we are not equipped with the men nor the machinery to get the most out of these things. While we have in this country abundance of raw material, it is a sad fact that most of it goes out of the country practically in a raw state because we are not equipped for the proper handling of it, nor the handling of it in such a way as to give the maximum of employment and money to our own people. Since the war broke out we have heard a great deal about the handling of nickel in this country. It was brought out last year that our nickel leaves this country practically in its raw condition, because we have not the technical knowledge nor the machinery to put it into an advanced stage of development. As nickel is a metal that is largely used in connection with the war, is it not a duty that devolves upon the Government, and a matter that comes within the scope of technical education, to see that we are in a position to handle that valuable commodity in such a way as to keep its ownership and its production within our own lines and in the hands of our own people?
The subject of technical education is very inviting and it is one upon which a great deal can be said. As I have already said, it is not a good answer for the Government to say: We have been speaking about this matter already and we will continue to dp nothing in regard to it. Even as a war measure, moneys of this country could not be better utilized than in educating our people to make the most of themselves and the most of the raw material that we have within our reach in this great country of ours.
[Mr. McKenzie. 1

I rise to express my approval of the question that is now before the House. This is a matter that has received the earnest consideration of more than one 'Government, >and the conditions ,of the country now are such that it is calling for the help and sympathy of every class of people in Canada. My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) is to be complimented for bringing this question to the 'attention of the House and of the country, and for many years n*)[DOT] question has come up fox consideration that seems to receive such unanimous approval as the question that we are dealing with now.
It is sufficient answer, however for the Government to say that its whole effort is now connected with the war and problems that come up for consideration in connection with the war. We have noticed the progress and development of the manufacturing industries of this country and I am sure the people of Canada agree that we have made great strides in that regard. Had the manufacturing industries of Canada not been in such an advanced position, we would have been unable to cope with the great questions that have come up and it would have been absolutely impossible for our manufacturing establishments to take hold of the manufacturing of munitions and other articles required in the war. I recall when the question of manufacturing in Canada-was a very heated one in the province of Ontario. A
5 p.m. Government in power many years ago in that province allowed trees to be cut into logs in the province and then allowed them to be sent over to the United States to be cut into lumber. The question became a live issue in the Legislature in the province of Ontario, and later the Legislature agreed that such a policy was not in the best interest of the people of that province, and the result was that shipment of logs out of the country was prohibited and those handling them were required to cut the logs into lumber in the province in order to give employment to the people of Ontario. All that is along the line of progress in manufacturing, and I am pleased to say, looking over the House and having had some experience and listening to this question being discussed, that every hon. member is interested in this question, and I think almost every hon. member will agree with me and also with my hon. friend the Minister of Labour when he says that in his opinion and in the opinion of the Government, the war is of

such importance that this matter can be delayed a little longer. For my part, I approve the question; I believe it is worthy of our best consideration. It is a matter that has Engaged the attention of the Legislatures of the different provinces throughout the country and it is one which should receive the consideration of this House and of the people of Canada and must be dealt with by this Government in the near future.
Mr. E, M. MACDONALD (Pictou): Mr. Speaker, the House might profitably discuss this question with great seriousness and care for some time with a view of having early action taken by the Government in regard to it. One of the problems which are continually engaging the attention of the press is the question of what Canada is going to do after the war, and a great many ideas have been put forward from a great many sources as to what will be the groundwork of the prosperity and advancement which we hope will come to Canada some day. Some hon. gentlemen tell us that immigration will come here, but immigration depends to a large extent on the question whether Canada is a cheap country to live in and whether we are able to offer to those who come from other lands such inducements in regard to satisfactory conditions of life as will enable them to come to this country with the feeling that they are able to do better here than.elsewhere.
There is, entirely apart from immigration, a question that intimately concerns every citizen of Canada at this time, and that is whether we are doing our full duty with reference to our institutions so that we may prepare conditions in such a way that the young men who are growing up and who have not been able to go to the war may be fitted in the best possible manner to take their place as citizens of this country, and that those who have gone and fought and who have returned may be equipped in the best possible way for pursuing satisfactory avocations which will enable them to earn a living and be of some assistance in increasing the wealth of the country. We can eliminate from the consideration of this question the elaboration of agricultural conditions, and we must approach the con. sideration of what is best to do in order that the industrial life of Canada in the future may be prepared for and made certain.
There is only one way of meeting future conditions, and that is by preparing for the
education of the young men who are growing up to-day, and giving them the best facilities for the development of whatever ability they possess. Are we doing our best in that respect in Canada? This Parliament, as the national body, is hound to assist in every possible way, and if we are not doing our whole duty then it is well that we and the people of this country should realize it. I think the motion of my hon. friend that the time has come when we should implement the recommendations that were made by the commission three or four years ago is a very proper one, and should receive the approval of this House. This is not a matter on which the parties should divide. The Government should not hesitate for one moment in accepting the principles of my hon. friend's resolution. Either technical education is a paramount necessity, or else it is of lesser importance than other things. It may be that it is more important to build the Quebec and Saguenay railway and to make arrangement* with my hon. friend for Charlevoix (Sir Rodolphe Forget) by which $8,000,000 is paid out of the treasury of this country, than to1 do anything for technical education, and if that is the view of the Government it is just as well that the people of this country should realize it. It may be that it is more important to this country to spend over $14,000,000, as the Government has done in the last four years on the Hudson Bay railway, in regard to which we have the report of the commissioners who investigated the general railway situation in this country, and to keep on spending $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 every year on that road, which when completed will under existing conditions only add to the seriousness of the problem that confronts the whole people of Canada, than to provide money for the development of technical education. For myself, I do not think so. Last year we spent on capital and ordinary expenditures $15,000,000 on public works in this country, and about $7,000,000 of that was spent under the Public Works Department. It is true that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce comes to us and talks of thrift and cannyness and care in our personal expenditure, and that the Minister of Finance devotes a large portion of his time to giving homilies to the people of this country on thrift. I am not dealing particularly with that, except to point out the moral that if this country can afford to spend $7,000,000 on public works it can surely afford to

spend something on preparing for the technical education of the youth and men of this country. We have seen that it is not a question of money with the Government. They have no trouble at all in raising money for certain purposes. They have placed upon the Order Paper a Highways Bill with all the expenditures it involves, and if the Bill is to be on the same lines as the one submitted to the House some years ,ago the Government surely need conjure up no difficulties about the expense of a technical educational scheme. If technical education is as important as hon. gentlemen concede it to be, surely it is possible for the Government to save money in one of the two avenues I have indicated to assist the provinces in the development of technical education. Last year it was objected that there would be difficulty in the way of this Government giving any aid to the provinces for technical education, because there might be a conflict of jurisdiction. It does seem to me that that argument is most far-fetched. The Minister of Agriculture some years ago brought in a Bill for the development of agricultural instruction schools in this country. A sum of $10,000,000 was set aside, and a certain proportion of that has been granted to the various provincial agricultural institutions in Canada every year. Each province has its agricultural schools and systems of education, but the Minister of Agriculture has never found the constitution going to pieces when the Federal funds were thus diverted. If that is so, upon what ground can it be urged that a similar arrangement with the provincial governments with regard to technical education would give rise to a constitutional difficulty? My hon. friend admits that technical education is a splendid thing; he has no doubt at all about its value, but for the time being he cannot do anything on account of the war. Now, I have given one or two instances where the Government notwithstanding the war have found time to devote their attention and give assistance to projects not so meritorious as the cause of technical education. It seems to me, therefore, that their time might well be employed, in working out a scheme of assistance for technical education similar to the plan which the Minister of Agriculture has adopted with regard to agricultural instruction, and which he has been able to carry out without prejudice to the performance of his regular duties, and without detriment to the interests of the country.

We hear a great deal about the necessity for increased production in this country. But increased production should not be confined to agriculture. In all those industries in which our young men are engaged, and which might be called natural industries because they are indigenous to the country and we have special facilities for their development, there should be increased production. Many of these industries provide staple products which enter into the consumption of every home in this country, and from these industries tens of thousands of our young men have gone forth to fight. Many of these men when they come back from the war will be unable to resume their former occupations, and where are we going to get the trained men to take their places except through a system of technical education? The Government very properly have taken advantage through the Hospitals Commission of the facilities existing in the various provinces for vocational training and the poor boyis coming home maimed from the front are being given technical instruction so that they can earn a living in another and perhaps less onerous line of work. This, besides giving them an 'opportunity to lead a useful life, adds to the products of the country.
If we had not had the way prepared by the technical schools that are to be found in every province of, the Dominion, where should we have been in Canada in regard to fulfilling our great duty to our young men who are debarred from returning to their former employments? In view of the conditions, what greater duty could he laid upon the country, what higher opportunity could be afforded it, than to assist, if not to the fullest extent suggested by t'he commission at least to some extent, in order that there may be given in each of these institutions instruction and training to fit our young people for the battle of life, and also to develop industries which will be of the greatest value to the country? One does not need to elaborate the facts which have come to us in these latter days of the marvellous development achieved by Germany under its system of technical education. That nation, though cribbed, cabined, and confined practically within its own boundaries, as the result of the naval supremacy of our Empire, yet has been able, up to this time, to maintain itself by following lines of scientific production. Mr. Hoover, who has recently returned to the United States, and has been given the task of dealing with production in that country, and

who is familiar with the condition of affairs in Germany, tells us?-and the facts are enough to astonish us-that, as a result of the internal conditions of Germany they are able to supply themselves through their own productiveness for six months longer, notwithstanding that their country has been for three years ^encircled by hostile forces. The only reason for this condition is that they have applied science to every walk of life by means of technical education. Through this system they have reached the plain people in every part of their nation, and have enabled them to work out intelligently the scientific principles in reference to production which their investigators have discovered. What, then, is the lesson for us? We are a comparatively sparse population in this vast country, but our aim and ambition always has been that we might make in Canada those things that our people need. Are we going to give notice now to the younger men who are growing up and who have not been able to take part in the war that we are going to do nothing to fit them for the great economic struggle upon which this country must enter in the time of keen competition that is likely to come when the war is over? Or shall we see to it that our coming citizens shall be equipped to be efficient members of the working force of a nation within the Empire in competition with the rest of the world?
In view of these considerations, I say that the duty which my hon. friend from Rouville urges upon this House and this Government is one of such character that we might well refrain from expenditures, such as those to which I have alluded

expenditures which, if this were the time to discuss them in detail, I could prove to be unnecessary at this iime

and devote ourselves energetically to the work of equipping the men of the next generation, those who within the next twenty years will have the destinies of Canada in their charge. We are told that the Government has appointed a commission of experts to inquire into the best lines of industry for our people to engage in. But that commission has practically only got under way. The practical value of any recommendations that they may make will depend upon having the skilled workers to carry those recommendations into effect. If in a year from now we are still discussing this question, we shall face it under greater obligations in the way of increased public debt and so with greater difficulties before us. If this committee of experts is to report within a reasonable time, why should not
we prepare the men by technical training so that they may be ready to put into effect by actual production and in the quickest time those recommendations which we hope will be made as to lines to be followed for Canada's industrial development? I venture to say that there is no question which, among thoughtful people, interested in Canada's future, 'is regarded as of greater importance than that submitted by my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux). Members of this Government must have heard from men who have given thought to this question as to its importance, and the vital, imperious necessity for action. As they are guardians of the public interest, and guides of the destinies of the country in this crucial time, I submit, the Government will fail in their duty unless they provide at the earliest possible moment financial assistance for technical education; this they can give without unduly burdening the public by simply putting off such expenditures as those. In this way we shall in 'some measure prepare for the conditions which will face us when the war is over.

I shall only detain the House a moment. I am sorry that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) thought it well to import what might be regarded as a slightly partisan tone into a purely economic discussion. This question of technical education was brought before this House eight years ago. I do not think there is any question in the mind of any hon. member that technical education in some measure at least lies within the power of this Parliament. This question is as to what we are going to do. Eight years have elapsed and I think it is now time that some action should be taken.
As an illustration of need for action, I met the other day the head of a large industrial concern in this country and he told me that some short time ago he had required an efficiency expert for his business; being unable to get one in Canada, he had to go to the United States, where he found a former Canadian, who had secured his technical training in that country and who was most efficient in his special line. To talk of not being able to afford the expenditure which would be involved in taking the necessary steps to put into effect technical education in this country on a broad and liberal plan, is not, I think, a proper view to take. I do not think that a few million dollars expended for such a purpose should be considered at all when compared with
lm

the value of the return which this country, and the generation which is now growing up, will derive from the investment. We are asked to wait-to waif until the war is over. Mr. Speaker, opportunity and time do not wait and opportunity and time are now with us. I do not think this is a case in which we should wait. I do not think we are doing our duty if we do wait. We din not prepare for this war; we could not prepare for it because we did not foresee it hut, in the name of Heaven, let us prepare for the peace which we hope and believe is soon coming.

Mr. Speaker, I do not suppose there is a member on either side of the House who would controvert the view now very widely acquiesced in, that scientific education, technical education and manual training are necessities of the age. Then if they are necessities of the age, they are certainly necessities for young and growing countries like ours which have to arm themselves in every possible way for the keen contest of competition which lies before them, the extension of trade and the development of resources. We are not to-day ranging onr *selves on opposite sides as regards the necessity for this kind of education, and the benefits that will arise therefrom. We are not controverting the principle therefore, should we take a little different position from that of my hon. friend (Mr.-Lemieuxj who moved this resolution. The resolution is:
That in the opinion of this House action should be taken by the Government at the earliest opportunity with a view to giving effect to the recommendations of the Commission on Technical Education.
That confines action of the Government to that one particular channel, which has been hewn out toy the commission of experts which was appointed to investigate and which gave a very thorough investigation to the question, taking a wide range of countries and a wide range of experience, and embodying within the report a vast deal of most useful and practical information. But no matter how gifted that commission may have been, no matter how wide the investigation it may have carried on, we cannot assent to the proposition that all wisdom lies with any selected set of men. They have embodied in their report, as the result of their investigation, an immense amount of the most useful information, and then they set themselves to make recom-

mendations as to the methods which shall be employed, or the channels along which the assistance to toe given shall flow. There arises an opportunity for honest difference of opinion.
