The Government after it has thoroughly considered the report and availed itself of the information they have gathered, may agree with many things that the commission recommend, or on the other hand, it may disagree with certain others. If we pass this motion as it has 'been placed before us by my hon. friend from Rouville, there is no latitude given to the Government for the exercise of its own judgment in reference to the methods to he adopted or the assistance to toe given. We are tied down absolutely to give effect to all the recommendations of the Commission on Technical Education. That is why we, or why I, myself, in speaking on this matter, take an opposite view to that taken toy my hon. friend.
No man, on this side of the House, has raised a voice against the necessity for, or the advantage of, technical education and manual training in this country. I am not going to take up the time of the House in speaking on the reasons for this, for I think we have passed the stage when argument is required in support of that principle. It is a question now as to how it shall he done, as to when it is to toe undertaken, and as to how much assistance shall toe given. We must not shut our eyes to two facts bearing upon this subject. One is that technical education and manual training axe as much, if not more, the function of the provincial parliaments as they are of this parliament. By the Act of Confederation, the provinces were given the controlling power over education; but that has not been held to preclude the Dominion Parliament assisting them along this and other lines of education. The provinces themselves, I have always contended, and I think so yet, have the major interest in this matter of technical education and manual training, and provincial effort has not (been altogether wanting in this respect. We find throughout this 'Dominion, that provincial, local and municipal authorities have in later years taken hold of this question and have advanced it very materially. In Toronto one of the finest temples of technical education and manual training to toe found in any country has been erected toy the civic authorities, and it is now in full operation and doing most excellent work not only for the citizens of Toronto, but for others who may take advantage of its facilities.

I know of my own knowledge that in the province of Nova Scotia very effective steps * have been taken towards the promotion of technical education and manual training in different parts of the province. In Halifax there is a notable instance of the activities which are going on. The theory,
I think, is a tenable one: that the provinces have the prime interest; but the Dominion is also deeply interested through several departments of its Government. Trade and commerce depend upon the development of the resources and the production of the country, and so the branch of the Dominion administration over which I have the honour to preside has a very keen interest in the prosecution of this education. The Department of Labour also has an interest in the subject. Technical education and manual training undoubtedly affect production and commerce, but they have an even greater influence upon the character and prospects of the labouring men, particularly artisans, of the country. That is why the Minister of Labour has an interest in this matter. In the Department of Agriculture the same thing applies. The Department of Agriculture, in its desire for intelligent, scientific productivity-and I think we have long since passed the stage of thinking that agricultural productivity can be carried on in any adequate way unless you get down to the scientific principles which underlie it and have worked them out in the development of your agriculture-is also keenly interested in this subject. These are the reasons why different departments of the Dominion Government have a live interest in this matter, and why Dominion aid and the sustenance and support of this Parliament ought to be given to technical education.
Technical education and manual training looked at as instrumentalities towards better production and better development of our resources, and consequently the making of wealth in this development and production, is a fine thing and worthy of the support of provincial and Dominion Governments. But there is another phase which to me seems to be as important, if not more important, and that is the effect of technical education and manual training upon the character and development of the men who are trained under such a system. The difference of character, the difference of stimulus, the difference of ideal, which lies between the man who works mechanically and the man who works because he understands the principle upon which he is working and is creatively 'and constructively
carrying out his work on those principles, is as marked as the difference between the two polles. The man who simply works mechanically may do a good job, but he 'has dullness instead of alertness, he has lack of stimulating interest and force, and the effect upon the character, the work, the life, of the man who works from educated, scientific foundations and principles, creatively and constructively, can hardly be adequately measured. And so by the very fact of bringing the artisan, the labourer, down to the principles of his work and inducing him to work upon them constructively, technical education is a force added to the development of the country in the character of its workers and the character of the children and families of these workers.
I have no desire to prolong the debate, but I have a desire to keep the freedom of the Government in this matter. I do not think that we should be tied down to the narrow limits within which the resolution of my hon. friend does tie us. I propose that instead of taking this resolution of my hon. friend and tying our hands to a certain method which has been laid down by the commission, the Government should be allowed to retain its freedom of action, while not going one whit behind my hon. friend and the spirit of his resolution as regards the importance and the necessity of what he has advocated. I therefore move that all the words after " that " be omitted, and that the following be substituted therefor:
In the opinion of this House the promotion of technical education and manual training is essential to the proper development of the resources of Canada and the extension of her internal and foreign commerce, and that reasonable assistance should be given thereto at the earliest practicable opportunity.
That preserves an equal stand as regards advocacy of the principle itself, and an equal adhesion to that principle, but keeps what I think it is important should be kept; it keeps to the Government freedom of action as to the lines along which it should give assistance, and it also mentions and provides for the practicable opportunity when that can be given.
I have a word to add. I am not making a plea that, because the war is on and is not finished, therefore the Government is entirely absolved from giving assistance towards technical education and manual training. If this amendment is passed, it does not preclude in its terms, the Government, when it has the opportunity, fully

considering this subject, as we shall have to do when the Prime Minister and other members of the Cabinet who are not now here, return. It does not preclude in any way the giving, even at a very early period, of assistance with reference to this matter. The main point, I think, is clear to my hon. friends on both sides of the House, and that is that the purpose of my amendment is to preserve the freedom of the Government as to the methods and lines along which it may give assistance.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce has covered the ground pretty well; I wish to say just a word or two in support of the amendment. The fact that the Government could not accept the resolution of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) should not, I think, imply any lack ci sympathy or consideration on the part of the Government for the subject of technical education. Nor would it necessarily mean that the Government would not move in that direction. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said that this was a non-party question; to that I think we all cordially subscribe. He urged that it was the duty of the Government to adopt the resolution of the member for Rouville and to accept the principle therein stated. I maintain that if the amendment is carried we shall be accepting the principle of the resolution; moreover, it would not have been advisable to accept the resolution in its original phrasing. The resolution states that we should give immediate effect to the recommendation of the Commission on Technical Education.
At the earliest opportunity.

It states that that report should be adopted. The member for Pictou, although he wanted this resolution to be adopted in its entirety, let drop a sentence that showed the impracticability of adopting it. As a matter of fact, I remember very well that the discussion which took place in the House on this subject in 1909 was entirely on the question of industrial and manual training. I remember going over the discussion subsequently; not a single word said by any speaker during the whole course of that discussion had relation to the question, for instance, of agricultural training; yet more than half the report of the Commission on Technical Education deals with the question of agriculture. I do net say that that question

is not equally important, but- the recommendations of the commission did not amplify or carry out the intent of the discussion that took place in the House, which related entirely to technical education as applied to our industries. This I conceive to be the great want.
A further remark I wish to make-because it ought to be emphasized in our acceptance of the amendment instead of the resolution-is that it was specifically acceptance of the amendment instead of as stated by many of the premiers of the provinces that they accepted the Government's suggestion to appoint that commission only if its purpose was to be the gathering of information. The strongest possible argument was made on that subject by the Premier of Quebec, Sir Lomer Gouin, who said *
We are of the opinion, my colleagues and myself, that anything pertaining to public education-whether the subject be special teaching or general teaching-belongs to the provinces exclusively, and I want to write you so, in order that there may be no misunderstanding on that point. As, on the other hand, you give me the assurance that the federal authorities, in instituting a commission of investigation, would simply do it with a view to help the provincial governments by having collected information which they would later on put at the disposal of the latter, we see no objection to the appointment of such a commission.
Later, when the commission was appointed, it was specifically started that the report of the commission was obtained in order that it might be put at the disposal of the various provinces, who might deal with it as they saw fit. It was placed art the disposal of every province and my recollection is that not a single province has stated in definite terms to the federal Government whether they approve the adoption of that report. How, then, in the face of that fact, the resolution of the hon. member for Rouville could be accepted by this House, I cannot very well see. For instance, the report recommended an elaborate scheme for carrying out this work, involving the constitution of a Dominion development conference, a Dominion development commission, a Dominion development fund, a provincial development commission, a provincial development council, local urban industrial development boards and local rural development boards. It is quite obvious, therefore, that we should not, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, bind themselves to the specific recommendations contained in that report. One word with regard to what the hon.

member for Pictou said in reference to agriculture. It is perfectly true that we are helping agricultural education. We are doing this by recognizing the jurisdiction of the provinces and giving large grants in aid of the educational work of all the agricultural colleges in Canada. It is true that the same method might be adopted in regard to technical education, but it is quite evident that the provinces themselves-and I think the federal Government would not want to force it upon them against their wish-would not desire that this Government should lay down specific methods in regard to education, even if it were technical education.
The hon. member for Pictou laid a good deal of stress on a matter which is of great importance, and that is in respect to technical education for returned soldiers. I assume my hon. friend knows what has been done in that regard; ample provision is made under the Hospitals Commission, the various provincial Governments co-operating, for the complete technical education of any of our boys who come back from the front-as rightly should be done. The matter of what further steps the Government might commit itself to is one that merits a certain amount of consideration. There is certainly not a member of this Government-and I am sure there is not a member of the House-who is not in hearty accord with the principle enunciated in the amendment introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and, to some extent, in the resolution of the member for Rou-ville. For my part, I do not see how we could accept the resolution, but I am quite sure that the whole House will be in sympathy with the amendment, which, after all, adopts the principle which my hon. friend speaks of.
May I ask the hon. minister if his interpretation of the resolution anticipates action by the Government this session?

I do not think my hon. friend would expect me to answer that question, after what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said with reference to the return of the Prime Minister and others of the members of the Government.

If the Government would give some assurance on that question, I would feel like supporting the amendment. If we get an assurance from the Acting Prime Minister that something will be done during the present session, I think that would be satisfactory.

I will be perfectly frank with my hon. friend. I am not the Prime Minister of this country; I am only the acting Prime Minister. The Prime Minister and two of his colleagues have been away for a couple of months; we have not had an opportunity of discussing this question lately, and I do not purpose binding myself or attempting to bind the House down to any particular course. If it is specific definiteness that my hon. friends on the other side are after, they will find as much in my resolution as they will in the resolution of my hon. friend. He asks that action be taken at the earliest opportunity. Who is to say what moment is opportune for taking action? The Government, of course. I think my amendment is a little more specific, more practical and less academic than the resolution of my hon. friend. I bring it down to "the earliest practical opportunity," and I have already stated that that does not preclude the possibility of its being done this session.

The earliest opportunity meant during this session.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Just before six o'clock I endeavoured to extract a promise from my hon. friend (Sir George Foster) who leads the House, that some action would be taken on this important matter during the present session. I am not sure that I caught what he said. He addressed honeyed words to the House which probably meant that he fully intends to take some action. I think it would be in the public interest that he should do so, for the delay has been altogether too long. I have had the honour of a seat in this House for twelve years, and I think that nearly every year during that time this question of technical education has been before the House in some form or another. It became an urgent question with the last Administration and was pressed upon them by supporters who felt an interest in it. The result was that some time before they went out of office they appointed a Royal Commission on the subject, which commission has done honest and useful work. We have had in this country many Royal Commissions-as my hon. friends will agree, they have been as thick as blackberries in

autumn. But many of them have not been productive of great results. This one, however, is an exception. The Royal Commission dealing with the question of technical education has done splendid work and has brought in a report that has been recognized by every one in this country as a very able document. I do not say that this Government should adopt everything that the Royal Commission has proposed. Nor would the resolution proposed by my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) make that necessary. It is rather a technical view to take of the resolution to say that if it is adopted there is only one course for the Government, and that is to carry out all the proposals of the commission. The Government, of course, would be free to adopt a policy and that is what we want- we want action in this matter. Prior to the war, one excuse or another was given for doing nothing, and last year the Minister of Labour, as I recollect it, gave the war as the excuse. He spoke of difficulties on account of the revenue. I do not regard that as an answer. The Government have been free with the country's money in many other directions. Not later than last year we voted a very large sum-some $6,000,000-to the extension of the Quebec and Saguenay railway. I am not saying whether that enterprise is a proper one or not, but in importance it does not compare with technical education. I might mention also the Hudson's Bay Railway, on which we have already spent $17,000,000. Yet that enterprise is not urgent compared with technical education. It is evidently not a question of funds that is troubling the Administration. Besides, I do not think that much money would be needed for some time. I presume that a policy something like that which is carried out in the United States could be adopted here. The state is required to equip a technical school before any assistance is given by the Federal Government. Probably years would pass before some provinces would be able to claim a grant made with those conditions. So, the question pi providing a large sum of money at once does not enter into the problem. I know my hon. friend will agree with me that as a war measure this resolution is particularly important. It is admitted by everybody that, next to winning the war, the greatest question before the people of Canada to-day is the development of the country's natural resources we must have
[Mr. Sinclair.!
trained men; captains of industry are what we want in this country, and we have splendid raw material from which to make them if we give our boys and young men a chance to learn the duties of such leaders. The manufacturers t-hemse1 ves have recognized this, and some have taken practical steps to meet the situation. The town in which I live is the headquarters of the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company. That company encourages its boys to attend the local technical school, and even goes so far as to say to a boy: If you will put in so many nights in a week in that school, it will count on your working time, and you will be paid for it as an apprentice. The boys get through their apprenticeship earlier by attending technical schools. I suppose the same method is followed in other places. This shows the great importance that the manufacturers themselves attach to technical education. I shall not weary the House by dwelling on that, because every one admits that this matter is of vital importance to the people of this country. Both sides have agreed that it should be taken up, and the only question that remains i3 as to when a start should be made. I can see no reason myself why there should have been such a long delay. While my hon. friend may not be able to tell us to-night, without consulting his colleagues, that he will bring down an estimate this session for the development of technical education, if he will say that he will recommend such an appropriation to his colleagues and will use his great influence at the council table,
I shall be satisfied, and I have no doubt that he will be successful. But I am very loth to part with him on this occasion without something definite because we do not want to have to go home and tell our constituents that the question of technical education has been brought up in the House again, and again postponed to a more convenient season. I think that is all I have to say. I am heartily in sympathy with the movement. I felt at first that if my hon. friend did not agree to a prompt step being taken it might be necessary to move to strike out the last words of the amendment and substitute therefor " during the present session of Parliament." But I do not wish to divide the House on this question, as we are all agreed on the general principle. I trust that my hon. friend will give us some more definite assurance than he has given us yet, that something will be done this session in this direction.

Mr. Speaker, I feel like congratulating the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) fo<r the courage and the extraordinary steadfastness of purpose he displays on all occasions, as well as for his activity at every session; his example should be followed by all the members of this House.
I have always taken a great interest in education, and I think the present question, should draw, at this time especially, the attention of the whole country. More than ever before, should we all realize the great necessity of education as an .asset in life. The idea should be spread throughout the length and breadth of this country, and no more ought we to hear in some remote parts that the people should refrain from electing educated men as school trustees because forsooth they know too much. Those ratepayers may be of the same mind as the judge of whom a member from the province of Ontario spoke this afternoon. This colleague went almost to the length of stating that he had heard the judge in question say that all members of the Bar were thieves. In that case, if that be true, I thank Heaven that I never was minded to become a lawyer.
To return to the point, I examined to some extent t'he report of the commissioners who investigated the question of technical education. It is so voluminous that I have not yet been able to go through the whole of it. But from what I heard this afternoon from speakers on both sides of the House, the commission has made practical suggestions which may help us to develop a system of technical education. After being elected to a seat in this House, I made inquiries from the heads of the various departments and was informed1 that in many instances men had to be brought from outside countries to fill positions that required technical ability. I was both surprised and grieved that in this country we had to seek elsewhere for men that we should be able to educate ourselves. That explains why I was impelled after the outbreak of the war to call the attention oif the House to the fact that there were Germans in our Civil Service.
Hear, hear!

I contend that in our educational institutions, where men are prepared for scientific pursuits, less time should be given to the study of the Greek and Latin authors and more to science proper.
All the members, those at least who have taken part in this debate, agree upon the necessity of our taking some action along the lines proposed by the hon. member for Rouville. At the same time it was suggested that it might be better for the present to devote our efforts to the objects of the war and postpone until after the war the question raised by this resolution.
On that account I believe the amendment of the Minister of Trade and Commerce should be adopted without a dissenting voice. The hon. member for Rouville himself will acknowledge, from the fact that the Government willingly accepts the principle of hi.s motion, that the amendtnent is timely and should be concurred in unanimously.

I was interested in this question when it was before the House last session, and I wish to say just a few words now. I have seen some of the benefits of technical education in the province of Ontario, where the Department of Agriculture has established a system of district representatives, and I am glad to know that this system is being extended to the other provinces. Seeing the benefits that have accrued to agriculture, the Dominion Government has thought it wise to give specific grants to the provinces, to be used for certain definite purposes. I have here the report for 1915 of the Ontario Department of Agriculture, by which I see that $114,000 was spent through the district representatives. I presume that that amount represents the cost to the provincial government of maintaining the representatives in the various districts. In addition to that, $20,000 was expended to encourage agriculture in schools within the province.
This sum I presume came largely from the aid given by the Department of Agriculture. It seems to me that my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture acted very wisely when he introduced his Bill to give agricultural aid to the provinces and, in connection with it, to direct, as far as possible, the expenditure of that money along lines that would be educational. I take it that the Department of Agriculture has appreciated the need of practical education as applied to agriculture and we have seen good results from the expenditure of this money. In the province of Ontario, during the short time these appropriations have been available and district representatives have been prosecuting their work, increasing interest in improved methods of agriculture has been shown by the farmers. I remember that when it was first proposed

to undertake such work within the county of Middlesex, the county council, at three successive session's, refused to accept the conditions under which a district ' representative might be placed in their midst because it wpuld require a paltry appropriation of $500. I do not think it was the size of the grant that affected them at all but I believe that the farmers at that time had the impression that a district representative amongst them would be more of a nuisance than a help, that he would not be of any real value and they did not seek to encourage the movement. But, when finally it was presented to them, they adopted the principle and asked the Government of Ontario to place a representative there. It was soon found that the demands on that representative's time were so great amongst the farmers of the district that a second man had to he appointed to assist him and within two years a third man was necessary. The m.ore the farmers avail themselves of the opportunities extended to them through the district representative the greater will be the demand for assistance of this kind. I am sorry to say that as a result of the war, possibly through enlistment of those who have 'been engaged in this work, although the need is as great as ever, it has been found almost impossible to get enough men properly trained and equipped to satisfy the demands of the different counties. In Middlesex to-day one man is doing the work, and he is quite unable to satisfy the demands made upon him. He can only skim over the surface of the work. But, no doubt, when the war is over and more men are trained for this work, we will find that the Government will be willing to give the farmers further help by supplying more men where needed.
In connection with technical and scientific instruction in agriculture in Ontario and the appointment of district representatives, a very important movement has taken place in the initiation of the acre profit competitions within the province. During the winter season classes are held in the high schools at which young farmers and the older ones too, if they care to attend, have the opportunity of hearing lectures on agricultural subjects by the district representatives. To encourage the movement further the Government of the province established the acre profit competitions. A significant thing in connection with these acre profit competitions is the great difference between the minimum pro-

duction and the possible maximum production even amongst those who took part in the competitions. In an acre profit competition in which the crop grown was potatoes, I find that in the Muskoka district one young lad produced, in 1915, 514 bushels of potatoes at a cost to him of $42.02. With the good prices prevailing that year he was able to reap a net profit of $336.72. In Renfrew county, Percy Wright in the township, I presume of Westmeath, produced 421 bushels of potatoes at a cost of $42.09 and with a net profit of $269.81. It runs from 514 and 421 bushels down until the minimum production is reached in the county of Frontenao where 51 bushels per acre were grown by Roy Ewing of Elgin-hurg, with a net profit of $9.87. What I wish to point out is the great difference between the 'possible maximum production and the minimum production. That shows that in order to secure the possible maximum production in root and other crops instead of the average production we must adopt scientific methods of cultivation and the use of proper fertilizers. Therefore, scientific farming and properly applied methods would produce a very much larger proportion of wealth to our country if information on these subjects were more generally disseminated and acted on throughout the province. In connection with these classes of instruction at the high schools five competitions in growing silage corn were held in which young lads attending these classes took part. On the five different plots the average profit was $85.56 at a time when silage corn was worth $3 a ton.
When we take the maximum under that, which reached $100.95, and the minimum, which was only $21.32, again there is an illustration of the enormous difference between the maximum and the possible. It is not necessary to elaborate along these lines. I rise to say that I shall support the amendment of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster), because I believe he is sincere in what he says, and I do not think it is said with any idea of postponing action. I believe he is fully seized with the need for as early action as possible in connection with this movement. To support and justify that opinion, I have before me a copy of a speech delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the 18th of April, 1916. He was discussing the matters that were pressing on us at that time, and referring to the activity in our industries, and as a result the large amount of onr exportable products. He said:

Whilst we are glad to see the munition works doing their part in supplying the Empire with that which is necessary, whilst we are glad to have the money which comes as a sequence to the employment, yet all this is not beneficent and productive work and when it stops-yes, before it stops-well before it stops-the people of this country should be putting on their thinking caps, sizing up the situation and getting ready for the inevitable and important change that is to come. The first duty of this House and of the people of the country is simply to face that situation, to get right down before it, face it, think it out and be prepared with plans and organization as to what shall be done when the time arrives. That is the first duty of us all. In the next place, will you allow me, Mr. Speaker, to call your attention to another phase of the question, and that is: what are the practical things that can be done and to what extent are we doing these practical things?
One of the things that I think we ought to do, and we may well do, is to take stock of the situation in Canada as it will probably be when peace comes. What is it in the Dominion of Canada that we shall consume, that we shall find necessary for our daily wants? To what extent can that be produced in Canada, and to what extent must we depend upon outside countries for these supplies? First-and I am not going to labour the point, for I wish to finish my remarks by six o'clock-I think that the thing we ought to do is to sit down and take stock of the resources and of the wants of the country. And with this idea-that, knowing what we require, and knowing how much is produced by ourselves at the present time, and for how much of it we have to depend upon foreign countries, we may, in a business way, set ourselves as Canadians to the solution of the problem of our wants.
I think that in these expressions the minister at that time had in view the movement which he later put in operation for the establishment of a research department. I am pleased to say in connection with that department, and I congratulate the minister on his choice, that when it became necessary to find a chairman to preside over that commission they had to get a man born and bred in the county I have the honour to represent, the county of Middlesex. ' Professor MacCallum has a good reputation. He has, if I may use the phrase, made good; and I believe that the choice the minister has made will be found to be a wise one, and that much good will result from the development of this work. The minister further found that it was desirable, and I think that this was essentially part of the technical training, to arrange to train and equip men to look after our foreign commerce, to train men in languages and in the science of trade and commerce. He said:
At the present time I am contemplating the sending of a special trade commission to the United Kingdom, to France and to Italy. These will be different from our trade commissioners.
I am trying to select four or five business men of Canada-men of capacity, of practical experience, to a certain extent of expert knowledge in the different lines of industry to which they are or have been attached-who will form an honorary commission.
All through the speech he made at that time there is evidence that there was in his mind a keen sense of the needs of this country along the lines of industrial development, and, in connection therewith, of technical and manual training.
The minister further said:
An attempt will be made to co-ordinate the scientific and engineering factors of Canada along the lines of research and technical requirements intimately connected with production and with distribution. I think this is of prime importance to us in Canada. There is to-day in our universities, in our colleges, in scientific societies, and in individual laboratories, excellent resources and ability for chemical research, for all that kind of research which transfers from the laboratory to the factory what is absolutely necessary for the factory at this time, and what will be more necessary for the factory when the period of unexampled competition comes within three or four or five years from now. Science, knowledge, and information are as essential to a well-ordered and successful business as they are to the profession of the doctor or the engineer or any scientific man. Germany's great point of vantage was that her technical and scientific instruction had advanced to such a pitch and had disseminated itself so widely that it worked itself into the very grain of Germany's production and made them the powerful competitors that (hey (were. Britain,, Canada, Australia1 land other countries must not merely take a leaf out of Germany's book; they must sit down before that question and solve it by bringing the aid of scientific research, of engineering capacity, of technical power and expertness into the region of the farm and the factory and the business establishment, and incorporating together those essentials which ought never afterwards to be disjoined.
Then, I think something else should be done, and should be dbne soon. It may be that I have been criticised for not thinking that it should have been done sooner, for I have had many statements and suggestions made to me on that score. Men have written to me and men have said to me: What is your department doing all this time? Should you not get people together, and should you not have them thinking, making plans, mobilizing for the work of the future? Now, I looked upon that in a somewhat different light from some other people. My view was that there was a time at which such an attempt would have been premature. But things have developped by the very force of necessity. The work in Canada had first to be devoted to the furnishing of munitions and war supplies. That took all the energy, and, for the time being, all the thought, all the enterprise, and all the capital, that could be got. The demand was less in normal lines, and consequently less enterprise could successfully be devoted to ordinary production.
I attended a meeting in Toronto in February last of textile manufacturers from all

parts of the Dominion where textiles are manufactured. At that meeting different manufacturers spoke of the difficulty they experienced in. getting properly trained men to manage the departments of the various factories. The problem was 'before them just as it is before the House now of properly training and equipping men to take -charge of the different branches or departments of their factories. They proposed that textile institutes should be established in different sections in proximity to -the factories. The idea was that the country should be divided into sections and that-textile institutes should be established, not *in each factory town, but at convenient central points. It occurred to me then, and I am still of the same opinion, that in such a case as that, some action might be taken by this Parliament similar to that of the Minister of Agriculture in appropriating a sum to help the agricultural industry.
In the city of London, Ontario, we have just completed a technical school which will cost about a quarter of a million dollars, and as a result of the development of technical education in that city the cost of education has increased to such an extent now that the school taxes of the city amount to 33J per cent of the total taxation.
I fully appreciate the fact that the matter of education is left entirely to the provinces, but I argue that, as we have found a means of assisting the provinces in the matter of agriculture, arrangements might be made, before a general programme of technical education is provided, to assist such organization, for instance, as the textile industry in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture has evinced much interest in the flax industry, and has given it much assistance. I rather think that the Department of Agriculture might even assist the Flax Growers' Association and help them to secure an increased interest in the production of flax. In most of the provinces-
I do not say in all, but in a number of them-technical education is a live question, but the present arrangements for carrying on technical education are largely due to local endeavour, with a certain measure of assistance from the provinces.
I do not believe in the principle of granting sums to the provinces on a per capita basis; I believe aid ought to be granted by the Government in proportion to the endeavour made in the respective provinces. It would be inadvisable that any grant from the Government should cause the prov-
[Mr. Glass.!
inces to reduce the grants they are. at present making to the local districts to which they are giving assistance, but rather to supplement them.
From what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said this afternoon, I have not the slightest doubt that this matter will occupy the attention of the Government when the Prime Minister returns. A reference to the speech delivered by the minister in April last satisfies me that the Government will give the fullest attention to the subject, and I am hopeful that as a result of their deliberations some action will be taken during the present session. I believe that it would be unwise to accept the resolution of the hon. member for Rou-ville as he has placed it before the House. I trust that as a result of the discussion which has taken place, my hon. friend will not deem it necessary to press his resolution. If his faith in the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has suggested the amendment, is as great as mine, he will be satisfied that the Government is fully seized of the need for speedy action in reference to this matter and that effective aid will be given.
On that side of the House.

I mean on my right hon. friend's side. I 'am afraid that his good intentions on this question of technical education will receive just about the same support from his colleagues as his good intentions on the question of patronage received last year. When this question was brought before the House last year we had the same pious promise made-not by such a pious gentleman as the Minister of Trade and Commerce-but by the Minister of Public Works, who listened to the debate and who closed it by asking the member for
Rouville to drop his resolution and to accept the promise which he made on behalf of the Government that his colleagues would look into this question with 'a favourable eye, and that at no distant date a substantial amount would be placed in the Estimates in order to give full effect to the principle of my resolution.
I am afraid my hon. *friend is putting into the mouth of my colleague words that Hansard will not show that he said.

I would read from Hansard what the Minister of Public Works said, but at the moment I have not the volume here. I remember quite distinctly, not the ipsissima verba of the minister, -but that he asked me to drop my motion and to accept his assurance that the Government would see to it that the question of technical education would receive full consideration at the earliest moment.
The Minister of Public Works did not put it in that way.

I have not his exact words .because I have not the volume of Hansard before me. I will, however, give a better authority than the Minister of Public Works. This question is not a new one before the House, and I could give my hon. friend scores of names of my Conservative friends who, when they were in Opposition, were asking the Government of the day to take immediate steps and prompt action in the matter. I have here the report of a speech delivered by a gentleman who is now removed from this sphere of activity to the Senate. I refer to Mr. Crosby who was member for Halifax. Speaking on this question in 1909, Mr. Crosby said:
Shipbuilding has been referred to by the mover of this resolution. One of the good reasons for instituting a technical school in Nova Scotia is that we expect to have a shipbuilding- plant there very shortly and we hope- because our people are very apt and quick to learn-to have men competent to take charge of the principal positions in connection with that industry.
And in 1909 he urged upon the Government of the day to vote a large sum of money so as to give technical education the proper standing it should have in the country. My hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Macdomell), speaking in the same debate, dismissing all the objections that were raised against a grant being given to the Government of the day, said:



Even if the Government acted upon that suggestion and issued a commission, and then chose afterwards, in accordance with the recommendations of that commission, to go further and embark on an expenditure of money for the purpose, it could still be done in conjunction and in connection with the various provinces or municipalities in different parts of Canada, whose moneys or other assets could be joined with federal assistance.
Let us now take the case of another very prominent member. I gave this afternoon the very weighty opinion of the present Prime Minister who said that he was entirely in sympathy with the object that the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) had in view, and he added:
I trust action will be taken along the line he has suggested, if no other action can be taken, but so far as I am concerned, I would greatly and infinitely prefer that a more definite and practical and speedy action should be taken than that which has been suggested in this resolution itself.
You did not think so much of that opinion then as you do now.

The Minister of Labour of the day, the Hon. Mackenzie King, if I mistake not, moved in amendment, that a commission be appointed and the House voted on that amendment, and shortly afterwards, in 1910, an appropriation was inserted in the Estimates, and in the same year after the appropriation had been voted a commission was appointed and the best men in the country were
9 p.m. selected to compose it. That commission went to work in Canada and in about nine other countries, including Great Britain, the United States, France, Germany, Holland and, if I mistake not, Italy, and it reported. When the report was received, my hon. friend (Mr. Crothers) was in office and, as I stated this afternoon, instead of action being taken the report was shelved.

My hon. friend is quite mistaken in saying that the report was made and shelved. The report was used as It was intended to be used when the commission was appointed. The commission was appointed expressly to gather information for the benefit of the provinces, and that information, When put in the form of a report, was sent to the provinces, and the provinces said: We do not approve it.
That is not the conclusion arrived at by the commissioners, and it shows that my hon. friend has not even read their conclusions.

My hon. friend must have misunderstood what I said. That must have been my fault in not making myself clear. I did not say anything about what the commission said. I said that the commission was appointed by my predecessor, Mr. King, solely _for the purpose of gathering information for the benefit of the provincial governments. My hon. friend said that when the report was made I shelved it. I sent it out to the provinces just as Mr. King said it was intended should be done, and I asked them what they thought of it and they replied in substance that they did not approve it.
My hon. friend is simply playing upon words.
No.

The	commission was
appointed to investigate and report, and when such a gentleman as Professor Robertson, not to speak of others, takes the trouble of preparing a report comprising four volumes with an additional volume giving recommendations, that report should receive more attention than it has received from my hon. friend. Not one of the recommendations made by the commisr'oners were followed by my hon. friend.

Or	accepted by the
provinces.

What was the result of that investigation? This Government spent $150,000 on the inquiry. The principle has been approved by both parties in Parliament. It was approved by the present Prime Minister of Canada himself, as I showed from one of his own speeches this afternoon. And what has been the result? Mark my words, Mr. Speaker. We have here the Estimates of the Department of Labour for 1918, and we find "Industrial training and technical education, $1,000." One thousand dollars I That is the whole result of that long investigation. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour is willing to promote the cause of technical education to the extent of $1,000, and yet in the dying days of last session-
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend may
sneer. He sneered the other evening and got his answer from the other hon, member for Brantford. In the dying days of last session the Government, without consulting the rank and file of the party, came before the House with a scheme involving

the expenditure of $6,000,000 to help some distressed financiers in the province of Quebec.
And in Ontario.

As to this recommendation of financial aid made by Professor Robertson, let me illustrate, for the benefit of hon. members who represent the several constituencies of Ontario, what it would mean for each of the industrial centres of that province to have the money spent according to the recommendations of the commission. In an address on " Education for Occupations," delivered in 1915, Professor Robertson said:-
The people of Ontario could draw from these funds to the extent of over a million dollars annually, besides receiving from Dominion authorities the co-operation arid advisory help of highly-trained and experienced counsellors in starting new kinds of schools, as for example for textile workers-
I call the attention of my hon. friend from Middlesex East (Mr. Glass) to this:-
-and in the development of new industries. In Ontario there are thirty-nine towns arid cities each with a population of over 5,000. These contain a total population of 953,896. It is estimated that within seven years after the policy was well begun there would be in these thirty-nine places about 30,000 pupils in the schools for the education for occupations of those over fourteen years of age. These towns and cities would draw from the Dominion Development Funds up to $380,000 a year.
Then he goes on to give a list of the cities and towns of Ontario and what they would draw from this Federal fund. Ottawa would receive $34,000; Kingston, $7,500; Belleville, $3,900, and so on. I wish to tell the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) that his city, St. Thomas, would gain, something if he were to give a little of his attention to this important question. The city of -St. Thomas would receive annually out of the Federal fund $5,500.
What would London get?
It would get $18,500; Brantford, $9,000, and Hamilton, $32,500.

I have not seen the report. Would the hon. gentleman please state on what basis these amounts are apportioned? Is it on the basis of population, or on the basis of expenditure by the local authorities?

Professor Robertson
says:
Under the policy recommended by the Commission, there would be two Dominion Development Funds to aid technical instruction and training; one of $350,000 a year to promote prevocational training by means of experimental science, manual training, drawing, domestic science, and nature study; and the other of $3,000,000 annually to supplement local efforts in providing education for occupations for those who are past public school age.

I am glad to see the leader of the House (Sir George Foster) take some interest in these matters. I have lost all hope that the Minister of Labour will study the question and give it due consideration. A year ago I heard an address by Mr. D'Amour, who was at the head of the commercial mission from France that visited Canada and the LTnited States. In that address he dwelt upon this very question of technical education, showing how France had lost and how Britain had lost, against their common competitor Germany, during the last twenty-five or thirty years. I remember very well that he declared that the French Government and the British Government were aware that it is not too soon to give to technical education all the necessary aid and assistance to assure its success. And he'added: "The British and the French Governments will not be taken unawares when peace comes, as they were taken unawares when war was declared." Would that not naturally be the motto of a progressive Government? I am glad to perceive by the statesmanlike remarks made this afternoon by the right hon. leader of the House (Sir George Foster) that he will give to this question the attention it deserves. Under these circumstances, and hoping-in fact being absolutely confident- that during the present session a substantial amount will be placed in the 'Supplementary Estimates to promote the cause of technical education, I accept the amendment of the right hon. gentleman.

Amendment agreed to.
Motion as amended agreed to.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF MEN IN HIGHER OFFICES.
EMPLOYMENT OF MEN IN HIGHER OFFICES.
speechtext: That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should decide that in the future, men only shall be employed in all branches of the Civil Service where, the salary is $800 or more, and that a Commissioner should be appointed to supervise the work done by the employees in each Department.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF MEN IN HIGHER OFFICES.
speechtext:
children lias a grievance. In support of my contention I may read a short statement from a government employee who earns $500 a year; he puts the situation in clea? light showing that $50 and even $600 or $700 are not sufficient at the present time to enable him to provide properly for his family. Here is a part oif his statement published in a local paper:-
"My salary is $500 a year, and as I had the misfortune of having been ill in the course of the year, I have received much less than that to live with, during twelve months.
I have been wearing the clothes with which I am clothed for three years and I have no better ones, and but for the close care of my wife, who is sewing and patching constantly, you would see me in tatters. Yet those clothes bought on credit three years ago, are not all paid for.
As long as I could get credit, the distress was less cruel, but now the creditors seeing no indication of any rise in my salary, refuse to advance to me any more, and even despair to ever recover what I already owe them. As a consequence, I am forced to beg from my friends, my relatives and my neighbors to make up the deficit in the pressing needs of my household.
I have my old octogenarian parents, to whose existence I am bound to contribute; i am deprived of the possibility to accomplish that sacred duty, and the poor old ones are suffering thereby.
We are often prevented from going to mass on Sunday, owing to the lack of the required fee.
I have to walk an average of fifteen miles every day to attend to my work and I cannot once dispose of five cents to take a car to allay my fatigue.
I cannot, as every citizen is called upon, and is bound to do, contribute to the various relief funds and to other charitable organizations, being myself a beggar; I cannot, in short, fulfill my obligations towards my religion, my family and the community-I am an outcast.
In addition to my duties as messenger, I am compelled to work assiduously as a clerk, but I am not paid one cent for that extra work.
My wife is sick and in constant suffering, since several months, and I can't provide any medical assistance to alleviate her painful condition.
Oftentimes in cases of sickness in my family, the doctor whom I could call without having any ready cash for him, prescribed some medicines that I could not get for want of money, and I still have in my possession several prescriptions not filled, to testify to this assertion."
I then asked this man what would be the monthly cost for the strict necessaries of his family, and here is the synopsis he prepared, and which I found very modest and without exaggeration:-
Rent	 $14.00
Fuel	 7.50
Groceries	 12.00
Meat and	fish	 10.00
Bread ..		 1.75
Milk	 96
Lighting	 50

Church	$ 0.50
Payment on furniture	 5.00
Sundries	 2.00

Monthly salary	41.66
Deficit	$12.55
Now, this messenger has no children going to school, what can be the situation of the one who, with such a salary, has three or four of an age to attend school?
Again, we must not forget the clothing, the shoes, the hats, the doctor and the medicine in case of sickness, and which are not mentioned in the above statement. Alas! If death should happen to strike at such a door, in what distressing condition would that family be situated?
In what sad circumstances would this poor wretch leave his wife and children if he happened to vdie; his salary being insufficient to enable him to live, he is far less in a position to pay insurance premiums on his life, or contributions to any benefit societies.
And that is, Mr. Editor, the deed of a Government whose mission is to protect its subjects, a Government having established a department to look after the welfare of the working classes in protecting them against the ambition and the injustice of the employers and contractors, and who itself turns a deaf ear to the lamentation and the pressing solicitations of its own functionaries, here in our Capital, in denying them what they have so legitimately the right to claim, their living and nothing else.
What efficient performance of his duties can we expect from a half starved and half clad servant deprived of all indispensable comforts of living? Here I will protest most vigorously, not only in favor of the messenger, but in the name of the whole community, because the country cannot be getting the efficiency in the public service as it would get from well paid men, free of all moral and physical care.
This state of affairs is inconceivable, it is barbarous, and moreover it is a disgrace for the country, and especially when we consider that certain classes of the same service are so liberally paid and live so sumptuously.
Now, come, honorable ministers and mdhibers, stop for a moment and reflect, look from the midst of your abundance into that chilly and denuded home of your servant who is giving all his time and all his intellectual and physical energy to the country, and if you have a soul and a conscience susceptible of compassion and equity, you will be eager to do justice and at the same time perform an act of humanity by granting to that neglected portion of civil employees a sufficient stipend to enable them to live and thus bring into the homes of these families relief and happiness, peace and cheer, and you will be praised.
Mr. Boulay continues in French: (translation): I am aware that the Government intends to do something for the employees who earn small salaries; there are too many highly paid officials to maintain in a state of poverty numbers of their fellow-workers. Let us take from the salaries of it he women, if necessary even from the

salaries of the higher officials; I do not believe in paying excessive wages. We could dispense with the services of any one who thinks his salary is too low when he gets $4,000 ia year; pult some ooe else in his place who will be satisfied with a fair remuneration.	.
I repeat what I said; those who get the higher pay are those who have less work to do. They reach the office about eleven o'clock in the morning and work only four hours a day. In cutting off -from some salaries and adding to others, the Government would be really helping the unfortunate ones who live in hard circumstances and who are after all the real painstaking employees and who give to the country not only their money but very often their life. The highly paid official is not anxious to enlist.
As I said, rtbe Government intends to raise the salaries in the lower classes of the service; well the sooner that is done the better for those employees who have suffered too long already. I know some married men who are paid $650 and who have told me they could not meet their monthly expenditure. The cost of living has abnormally increased especially this year and there is no doubt that those employees should receive at least $800, if not more.
iMy resolution calls for the appointment of ia commissioner to supervise the work done by the employees in the various departments. It may be objected that there is no necessity for such an official as there are supervisors in the different branches of the service. iMy personal experience enables me to say that much time is wasted; I have seen with my own eyes some officials, with their feet on their desk, reading quietly a newspaper. I hold that the office hours during which they are paid to work should be devoted altogether to the public service; that is my reason for asking that a special commissioner be appointed to go the rounds and supervise the amount of work done by every one of the employees in each department.
I hope my hon. friends who speak another language have understood the plain meaning of my resolution which has reference only to the employment in the departments of ladies at high salaries. I have nothing to say about stenographers and young ladies who are ready to accept small salaries. I speak particularly of those whp axe receiving wages which would permit a man to support a family. That is the main point of my resolution and I think it should be
earnestly supported. I know that I will not have the pleasure of being favourably looked upon by the ladies concerned.

speechtext: You are a married man, are you not?

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF MEN IN HIGHER OFFICES.
speechtext: I am, but I propose this sincerely and in good faith because I think it is in the interest of our country.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF MEN IN HIGHER OFFICES.
speechtext:
What is. the Government's policy on this question? I assume that, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bpulay) has just stated, he is married and is not in the matrimonial market, he has no object to serve Iby being friendly with the ladies and certainly he does not expect woman suffrage to reach his constituency. Those of us who come from other parts of Canada where the women have been given the right to vote, have altogether a different viewpoint from that of the hon. gentleman. If that viewpoint weTe not superinduced by any other reason it wpuld be iby the fact that a large.and highly respected population, which the hon. gentleman wishes to decapitate officially will probably have in the near future the opportunity of marking their ballots for or against the members of this House. As all thinking men are very susceptible to public opinion I take it for granted that no member from the provinces where woman suffrage lias been established would think for a moment of supporting my hon. friend in Ms resolution. The question which he raises as to the ladies taking the places of men would have sounded better some years ago. To-day we have arrived at a situation in Canada, and in various countries of the world, where women are taking the places of men, and I am free to admit that in many instances they are taking them with as great ability as the men have displayed. I would go further and say that in many offices where the business of the country is transacted men will have to brace up or they are going to lose more of their positions. There is no business man who has in his employ ladies in different positions but will agree with me that during the past few years they have risen to such a high eminence in these positions as to make their services almost indispensaMe. My hon. friend raises another point as to the moral standing but there his argument limps. He argues that the presence of ladies in various public offices is not for the best ininterest of the country. Then he cripples that rather by saying that the standard will be higher if they are

not allowed to get better wages, that a lady will be all right at $800 but that if she. should get $1,200 the temptations would be greater. I take absolutely the opposite view. Then my hon. friend also says that the higher the' salary the less the officials work. Consequently he is going to give the high salary to a man and the low salary to a woman, let the woman do all the work and let the man have the high salary and none of the work. There is something in the contention that men with families ought to be given positions and I agree with him if they are fit for the positions. But the time has gone by when a man can sit around and say: You must give me a position because I am a man, if there is a woman in. sight to fill that position more efficiently. As to the salary, I am rather of the notion that work should be paid for irrespective of the party who performs the work and if a public office sees fit to engage a lady to perform certain services and she proves efficient, there is no reason under the sun why she should not receive the same .salary as the man who performs the same work. I am just simply taking some of the things mentioned by my hon. friend but I would point out to him that he will have to catch up with the procession by the time woman suffrage gets to the province of Quebec or he will find himself without any seat in this House at all. Now, what will the Government's policy be?

Whilst my hon. friend (Mr. Boulay) was speaking, I noticed the interested look on the face of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and the idea came to me of asking him to answer the argument of my hon. friend from Rimouski. My intuition proved true and my hon. friend from South Renfrew came to the mark in right gallant style. But I had always had the idea that a Frenchman was the embodiment of gallantry and it really took me quite by surprise that my hon. friend, here, who is a good

looking man and a Frenchman, should have had such an heretical opinion in respect to the ladies and especially to the young ladies. That is why I asked him whether he was a married man or not. I wanted to solve that difficulty. But I have another question to put to my hon. friend. The young ladies, he says, spend their money on the toilette, they buy things to make themselves look nice and to keep them warm. What do the men do? If I had a man in my office and he did not keep himself very well dressed and buy things that would make him look respectable, I think I would ask him, for the benefit of the office, to spend a little more on his personal outfit.
My hon. friend, who is not so young as he once was, was once younger than he is now. I *wonder if he, in casting his eyes oveT the young ladies of his locality when he was looking around for a wife, was not a little taken now and then with those who were rigged out nicely, who *wore nice hats and nice dresses. I venture to say that if we could go back and analyse these times, a little distant in the past now, we would find that 'he had an eye for the beautiful in that way just as all Frenchmen that I ever knew anything about have had.

speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Boulay) has placed his views before the House. I think I am not stating what is incorrect when I say that the Minister of Finance is cogitating over a measure by which at least the lower grades of the service shall have some addition to their salaries, and when that Bill comes before the House, as I think it will, my hon. friend can advance his arguments to the Minister of Finance. But I am afraid I wall have to tell him that he will not get far with the Minister of Finance if he pursues exactly the same line of argument that he has pursued to-night as against the young ladies.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF MEN IN HIGHER OFFICES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be untrue to the best traditions of my race were I to leave it to an English-speaking member to enter the lists as the champion of fair ladies who have been subjected to .attack by a representative of my own province, the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay). My hon. friend is opposed to ladies being employed in the Civil Service. Why draw a line between the government service and the many other fields of activity in this country of ours? In every branch of

industry, in all commercial pursuits, in professional avocations, in the offices of insurance companies, are to be found young girls and ladies employed as stenographers, clerks and accountants; hon. members who belong to the legal fraternity especially will bear me out when I state that women always give entire satisfaction, that they are even looked upon as the most efficient workers. Why then should they be debarred the service of the Dominion
I wish to point out to my hon. friend that most girls do not seek employment to shut out the men. In most cases they are impelled to look for work by pressing conditions. Their .situation is not of their own choosing, and many of them, should a man offer marriage, would willingly leave their position to which they cling from sheer necessity.
There are many young ladies who are alone to provide for the support of a widowed mother and younger brothers and sisters, for whose education they also pay out of their salary. Why, I repeat, in the Dominion Civil Service should they be discriminated against any more than in commercial, industrial and professional spheres?
I would, however, feel disposed to support the hon. member on his stand regarding determined bachelors. I do not go the full extent with him and suggest they be dismissed from the service. I am not in favour of taking such drastic action, but if he moves to have them taxed- or visited with some other like punishment, I shall not stand in -the way of his motion. The hon. -member takes a wrong position when he puts the -unmarried men on the same footing as the- unmarried women of the Civil Service. The men have the choosing of their career and can change it at will; many girls on the other hand would -readily take to matrimony if they had the choice.
In a word, I believe the hon. member made a false move when he brought in this resolution and he must now be satisfied that it will not enlist the support of the House or obtain approval in this country. As stated by my hon. friend for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), women on many occasions proved themselves the equals of men; they are now proving it by the material help they are giving in connection with all the undertakings o-f the war in Europe and especially in Canada. To my mind, the hon. member for Rimo-ufki's motion is most untimely.

Mr. Speaker, I sympathize with my hon. friend in only one phase of his remarks, that is with reference to the salaries of the lower grade civil servants, especially the married men of those grades. I have said on other occasions that I oould not see how it was possible for a man to bring up a family on a salary of $500 or $600 a year, and I am glad that the leader of the House has announced that the Minister of Finance (Sir Thom-as White) is contemplating bringing in some legislation in the near future to relieve the situation for the lower grades of the Civil Service. I believe there is top much disparity in the salaries of civil service employees as between the higher and lower grades. There should, of course, be some disparity because the work done by the higher grades is more important and is deserving of better remuneration. But still the salary of any civil servant should be sufficient to provide a living wage, and a man should not he crippled, should not have his family almost starved, because he is in one of the lower grades of the service.
I shall say nothing further now) but shall wait until the measure is brought do-wn by the Minister of Finance. I hope he will -make sufficient provision in that measure fo-r the lower grades of the Civil Service.

That, in the opinion of this House, in consideration of the present pressing need for national economy, a Committee of nine Members of this House be appointed, five to be named by the Acting Leader of the Government and four by the Leader of the Opposition, who shall forthwith consider, and during the present session report to this House the total cost, including incidental expenses, of each Session of Parliament, and the best way, if any, of reducing the same, with power to send for persons and papers.
He said: I do not think, Sir, that it is necessary for me to occupy the time of the House at any length in supporting this resolution. In the absence of the Finance Minister I may say that I spoke to him about the matter. He was in accord with the suggestion, and promised, if here, to speak in its favour when it came up.
Without making any charges against anyone, I think that at such a time as this, when thrift is being preached from the housetops, it is well that we'should look into the question of whether we can in -any

way'reduce the expenses of our meetings. Personally, I have a strong suspicion that in half a dozen different directions these expenses might be decreased. I happened to hear in the House the other day an answer to a question with regard to the expenses of Hansard; I merely give that as an illustration. The information given was that Hansard cost the country about $76,000 a year, -the translation costing $36,000. I am sure that it is possible in some way to reduce such an expenditure as that. Without going into details which are well known to every member of the House, 1 beg to submit this motion in the hope that the House will see fit to take this means of securing what has been -so much clamoured for throughout the country- economy-in our national expenditure.

I think we all agree that the motive behind this motion is a worthy one, and for my part I would not object, 'being -an old member of the House, to acting as a member of that committee with a view to shortening, if possible, the length of the session, which is admittedly too long. I am quite sure that my hon. friend has not in mind the curtailing of the privileges enjoyed by those of us in the House who speak in the French language. There is nothing in his motion which suggests that the outcome of any such investigation as is proposed, will be the curtailment of the privilege of the minority to use the French language -and to have the translation of the official documents and of Hansard. I have noticed in the press -some apprehension that the House might, in its wisdom, decide to do away .with the translation and with some of the official documents. With the understanding that this will not be the case, I heartily support my hon. friend's motion.
As regards Hansard, I do not know how we could do without it, though it might be possible to do away entirely with the reporting of the committee stage of the House, having only the main discussions, the debate on the Budget, for instance, reported. In that way you would reduce materially the size of Hansard and make it a little more accessible even to those who have contributed to the filling of its pages.
I wish to add this with regard to Hansard. I have had some experience in various countries, -and I believe that when you compare our Hansard with the English Hansard and with the Congressional Record which contains the reports of the proceedings in the United States House of Repre-

sentatives, and the official report of the debates in the French Chamber of Deputies, you will realize that we have a staff which can compare with that of any parliament in the world. But I am free to admit that the report is far too bulky and that it could be materially reduced in size, in the best interest of the country. Some of the blue-books, too, might be reduced in size. I pay this compliment to the King's Printer, Mr. J. de la Broquerie Tache, a gentleman whom I heartily recommended a few years ago as successor to the late Mr. Parmelee. I believe that Mr. Tache, and his assistant, Mr. Cook, have of late accomplished a very important reform. As you are aware, in former years a copy of each blue-book issued was addressed to each member of the House of Commons. Many of these blue-books, which were -costly, did not reach the members to whom they were addressed, or were not regarded as being very important. Many were neglected and, perhaps, finally sent to the waste-basket. Two years ago, Mr. Tache and Mr. Cook decided that upon the issuance of each blue-book a card should be sent to each member stating that the blue-book was available and that it would be forwarded upon application by the member. I think that was a very good reform, and it has worked wonderful results. Many members did not wish to have some of the reports which were issued by the King's Printer, and by the adoption of the new system the Government has saved a large amount of money. I dare say that other reforms of a similar nature could be made, in the matter of stationery, etc. On the whole, I think that my hon. friend is quite right in moving for the appointment of a committee to look into this matter. In these war times it is a worthy object to endeavour to decrease the cost of administration by reducing as much as possible the expense incurred in carrying on the affairs of this House.

Mr. Speaker, so far as this resolution goes, I think I may say for the Government that not only have they no objection to it, but they will be under -an obligation to the hon. gentlemen who will form the committee, if that committee will devote a portion of their valuable time to the work and give us the result of their deliberations and investigations. The figure that was named to-night by my hon. friend who proposed the resolution is certainly somewhat startling, and I have not the least doubt in the world that if the

committee, when appointed, set themselves to work, they will be able to find ways and means by which the efficiency of this House will not be diminished, but the cost of carrying it on, which now amounts to such a large'figure, may be very materially reduced. I do not wish to debate the question.
Motion agreed to.
