Might I call the attention of the Government to a matter which is of the utmost interest to the families of our soldiers. I have received this letter from a gentleman in Montreal whose son is at the front, and who is well known in public life as an advocate of land reform. I refer to Mr. Henry Timmis.
Westmount, 7th April, 1917.
My clear Mr. Lemieux,-
A matter which I should like to see you bring to the attention of the House is that of postage on parcels going to Our men in England and France. By merest coincidence, the son of the woman who does char work around our house is in the same battery as our boy, the 79th. Since her boy enlisted, her husband's health has broken down, her daughter has become an invalid, and so it has become necessary for her to work out two or three days each week for $1.50 per day. It is her custom to send over a box of comforts to her hoy each week or two. On some occasions the postage on these packages at the rate of 12c per pound amounts to nearly a dollar. If parcels were carried absolutely free there might be a disposition to send over unnecessary articles, but surely the Charges should he reduced by two-thirds.
I wish my right hon. friend would take up this question with his colleagues, because there is a hue and cry throughout the country against this rate of 12c. per pound upon parcels sent to our soldiers abroad. If my hon. friend will tackle this postal rate with his usual acumen and with his good heart, he will certainly receive the blessing of thousands of mothers, wives and sisters, who cannot afford to pay such a high rate of postage for sending comforts to their sons, husbands or brothers, or even sweethearts, on the other side.

subtopic: COMPLAINT AS TO THE RATE OF POSTAGE.
speechtext: I shall be very glad to call the attention of the Postmaster General and of the Minister of Militia to the matter, and consult with them in regard to it.
On the Orders of the Day:

I wish to call the attention of the right hon. gentleman who is leading the House this evening to a matter which I know will interest him. I wish to ask him if the Government will not consider the passing of a Bill to repeal the Canada Temperance Act in those eight counties in New Brunswick in which it is in force. I could introduce a Bill myself to that effect, but, of course,, at this stage of the session it would never reach a point where it would be discussed.
A year ago the legislature of New Brunswick passed a prohibitory law very much after the lines of the Manitoba and Ontario Acts, and it became effective on the first day of May of this year. There are eight counties in which the Canada lem-peranee Act is in force, and for its repeal the law requires a petition to be signed by twenty-five per cent of the ratepayers; then this Government orders ail election to be held, and if a majority of the electors vote in favour of a repeal of the Act the Act is repealed; but that entails a great deal of time and expense, and I believe that it would be well received in the province and would not do violence to any principle if this Parliament should repeal the Act so far as those eight counties are 'Concerned. I therefore throw out that suggestion to the right hon. gentleman and ask him if he will not consider the matter, and, if he thinks advisable, if he will not take the necessary steps to pass the required legislation.

I have had my attention drawn to this matter before, but it has always seemed to me that there are two difficulties in the way. In the first place, the Canada Temperance Act goes into force by virtue of the people's own vote upon it; they call for a vote under certain forms and they, get it. It is the action of the people themselves and not of the Government, and therefore, it is a question of some importance to know whether, if the Government arbitrarily undertook, by passing an Act, to get rid of the law and repeal it, they would be acting in conformity with the wishes of a majority of the people in the county or electoral district that had taken steps to put the Act into force. In the second place the law in New Brunswick, for instance, I suppose

supersedes in Scott Act counties, the Ssott Act provisions.
No, that is just the difficulty. It does not.

Then the situation is this: in those eight counties in the province of New Brunswick the provincial law has no force owing to the Canada Temperance Act being in force there, but I suppose the provincial law is of some assistance in enforcing the other Act.
No, it is entirely neutral

That remark of mine then may be left for what it is worth and it does not seem to be worth very much, so far as that is concerned. This, however, may take place-'it may be possible that the New Brunswick law, having been enacted by the New Brunswick Legislature can as easily be repealed, and then the Scott Act would remain and would be for the use of the people of those counties. There is a method by which the people themselves can get rid of the Act if they wish to come under the provincial law. It takes some trouble and it takes some expense, but in that way we should know it was the wish of the people themselves. That has been the consideration that has always come up when this question has been discussed before.

There is something in what the right hon. gentleman says, that in these eight counties this particular law was brought into force by the votes of the people, but he should not forget the fact that the prohibitory law was brought into force by the representatives of these counr ties. Therefore it is fair to assume that the votes of the people through their representatives enacted a law which they would like to have supersede the Canada Temperance Act, but unfortunately, as the Canada Temperance Act is in force by virtue of an Act of this Parliament, they have no power to repeal it.

That consideration goes a certain distance. It would be quite possible for prominent men in a county to form themselves into a committee calling for the enactment of the New Brunswick law, for instance, and yet they might not represent a majority of the county. When the voice of the people has been legally expressed, you have no right to say that that voice does not still prevail

until the people themselves take the legal methods of informing Parliament and the country that they now wish otherwise. On the other hand, this matter is before the Government and we shall certainly give it our consideration. If there should be some strong expression of opinion from these counties that would convince the Government that they really wanted to get rid of the old law and come under the new, the difficulty would be practically eliminated.
